usd3-3jane.title: Senior Credit Is Still Credit
usd3-3jane.text: USD3 packages 3Jane's senior credit tranche into an ERC-4626 share: USDC enters, idle cash waits in Aave, and the rest finances fintech receivables and crypto credit lines. Its NAV can rise above a dollar because interest accrues into the share price, so the familiar ticker is doing fund accounting rather than promising a fixed $1 quote. sUSD3 absorbs losses first, but that protection is only as thick as the junior tranche, and recoveries from an impaired off-chain borrower can take months or years. Nothing on the card moved this release, and the card is unusually candid about why the grade is not higher: the credit receivables are scored as receivables rather than folded into the dollar they settle in, so the liquid Aave buffer and the deployed book are priced apart instead of averaged into a comfortable middle. That separation is the whole point, because the buffer, the exit route, and the unit of account are all the same dollar. A haircut upstream would reach every part of the structure at once. The senior seat is safer than the junior one; it is still a claim on 3Jane's credit book, not on the dollar it settles in.

kusd-kerne.title: Base synthetic dollar with USDC PSM
kusd-kerne.text: kUSD is Kerne Protocol's Base-native synthetic dollar. A first external audit from Hexens landed in late July with zero criticals and every finding confined to the yield vault. The audit followed a patched Peg Stability Module cutover that opened permissionless 1:1 USDC minting. Circulating supply remains genesis-scale dust across a handful of holders. DefiLlama indexes the supply with no usable price, and CoinGecko still does not resolve the coin, so Pharos keeps it on the upcoming tracker. The live KerneVault still runs pre-audit bytecode with deposits closed until the remediated version deploys, so the audited code and the deployed code are not yet the same thing. Current backing is USDC in the PSM contracts, covering outstanding kUSD slightly above 1:1. The ambitious delta-neutral design, using a WETH vault and Hyperliquid short, remains degraded and excluded from reserves. Admin authority sits with a 2-of-3 Gnosis Safe, and hourly signed proof-of-reserves is published at kerne.fi/verify. The durable constraint is distribution: the protocol keeps shipping before users arrive.

usdt-tether.title: Treasury-Heavy Dollar Base
usdt-tether.text: USDT's A+ overall grade is the sound of scale winning arguments: an A+ peg record, an exit pillar scored at the very top of the scale, and economic control landing in A- territory. Backing is the lone B, with secured loans, gold, bitcoin, and equities alongside the Treasury wall. The Q2 2026 BDO attestation keeps assets ahead of liabilities, but the excess reserve buffer nearly halved in a single quarter to roughly $4 billion, a rounding error against a book of well over $180 billion and exactly the line skeptics will watch as gold marks and bitcoin swings flow through it. USDT0 extends the franchise across another wave of chains through lock-and-mint rails, useful for distribution and a reminder that omnichain convenience is not the same thing as issuer decentralization. The redemption floor is real for eligible Tether customers, but it remains governed by Tether's terms, discretion, and quarterly attestation cadence rather than continuous bank-style disclosure. The franchise's two faces stay on display: when OFAC attached 131 TRON addresses to its ISIS-K designation in July, Tether froze every one within hours. This sanction-machine reflex is faster than a bank's response. In Europe the MiCA wall keeps rising, with Revolut set to delist USDT for EU users by the end of August 2026 and force-convert whatever remains. The 2019 accidental 5B mint is still the canonical lesson: the biggest stablecoin can be operationally serious and structurally centralized at the same time.

sources.label: CoinDesk: Tether Q2 2026 attestation ($1.5B operating profit, reserve buffer falls by half)
CoinUnited: Revolut delists USDT for EU users by August 31, 2026 under MiCA

usdc-circle.title: The Institutional Default
usdc-circle.text: USDC is crypto's compliance-first reserve currency: cash and cash equivalents sit in the Circle Reserve Fund, managed by BlackRock and custodied at BNY Mellon, while monthly Deloitte examinations reconcile assets and liabilities. This release re-anchored the curated composition to the June 30 examination and Circle's live transparency feed still resolves cleanly against it. Short-dated Treasuries carry most of the weight, with overnight reverse repo and bank deposits split by systemic importance underneath. Every pillar finished exactly where it started. Its on-chain liquidity is unusually distributed, so a dollar that exits one venue does not have to leave the market altogether, and the SVB weekend remains the reminder that banking access can still interrupt an otherwise conservative reserve stack. The A+ is doing a narrow job: it says the reserve and the exit are about as good as this asset class gets, not that the ordinary weakness went away. That weakness is still the point of centralization: direct {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} runs through Circle, and Circle can control the token. USDC is intentionally boring infrastructure, provided the gatekeeper and its bank-and-fund chain remain boring too.

dai-makerdao.title: The OG Decentralized Dollar
dai-makerdao.text: DAI is MakerDAO's decentralized USD stablecoin: {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-minted origins, now mostly backed by PSM stablecoins and Sky's allocator books. DAI is the stablecoin that proved crypto could create a dollar without a bank account, and the A- report card still rests on genuine DAO governance rather than a multisig cosplaying as one, though the V9 economic-control pillar grades that machinery a B, a reminder that even the OG DAO keeps levers someone can pull. The reserve composition has drifted far from crypto-purist origins: roughly 40% other stablecoins through the {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}, Grove's institutional-credit and Spark's lending allocations near a quarter each, and only a single-digit sliver left in the crypto vaults that made DAI famous. It is functionally a hybrid fiat-credit dollar. The peg score sits in the mid-nineties, and the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop, powered by atomic PSM access at zero fee, earns a near-perfect exit pillar, more than almost anything else on the dashboard can claim. Now overshadowed by its own rebrand as USDS, DAI occupies a strange position: still billions in circulation, the philosophical North Star of decentralized money, increasingly backed by the centralized assets it was designed to replace. CDP vaults remain the original minting path.

frax-frax.title: From Algorithm to T-Bill Basket
frax-frax.text: FRAX abandoned its {{term:algorithmic}}fractional-algorithmic{{/term}} origins to become a tokenized {{term:treasury}}T-bill{{/term}} basket with clean reserves, scarred history, and an awkward middle ground. The current balance sheet leans on Frax-owned liquidity, WisdomTree WTGXX, Superstate USTB, BlackRock BUIDL, and a smaller Ethena/Convex strategy sleeve, which is a long way from the reflexive coin that once made the brand famous. The reserve reads like an institutional allocation, yet the report card still treats the dependency stack and old peg scars as unresolved baggage rather than ancient history. FRAX sits in the uncomfortable middle: too decentralized-dependent for institutional comfort, too TradFi-backed for DeFi purists. A wide spread of DEX pools sounds impressive until concentration math and merely passable liquidity undercut it. The yield via Vesper lending barely compensates for that ambiguity; you are not being paid much to hold a stablecoin still arguing with its own origin story.

tusd-trueusd.title: Transparency in Name Only
tusd-trueusd.text: This release did two notable things to TrueUSD and neither of them touched the grade. Moore CPA was corrected upward from a niche attestor to a regional one. It was a genuine promotion, earned by daily individually signed reasonable-assurance reports that most issuers could not sustain for a week. And the composition behind those reports is now documented: effectively the entire reserve sits at cost in a single First Digital Trust fund position, in instruments the attestor's own notes concede cannot be readily converted to cash, against a backdrop of redemption litigation and a worldwide freezing order. The scoring model cannot see either fact. The record is typed as real-time proof of reserves, so Pharos never consults the independent-static path. That path is the only place attestor tier is ever read. The near-total single-counterparty concentration lands on a backing pillar already priced for opacity, so the C stands exactly where it was. A daily {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} of a reserve you cannot get out of is the most precisely measured illiquidity in the asset class, and TrueUSD survives on institutional inertia rather than anything the name still promises.

lusd-liquity.title: The Immutable Benchmark
lusd-liquity.text: LUSD remains the philosophical standard for decentralized stablecoins: ETH-only collateral, immutable contracts, no admin keys, no governance, no upstream dependencies. The design earns near-perfect marks on the exit and economic-control pillars, while the same ETH-only purity keeps backing a notch lower and holds the overall grade at B+ rather than the A its reputation implies. The permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop is the load-bearing piece, providing a hard floor at $1 by letting anyone swap LUSD for $1 of ETH from the riskiest Trove in exchange for 50 bps. The hundreds of recorded peg deviations reveal the trade-off of purity rather than weakness: ETH-only backing at 110% minimum pushes borrowers to hold safety margins, producing persistent above-peg drift, and every ETH crash tests the Stability Pool's absorption capacity in real time. Supply keeps slowly bleeding, down more than an order of magnitude from its 2021-era peak. This is the fate of a v1 protocol overshadowed by its own successor BOLD, which added multi-collateral support and user-set interest rates. LUSD is increasingly a monument rather than a market participant. It is the stablecoin that proved decentralization works and then watched the market choose convenience anyway.

mim-abracadabra.title: Battle-Scarred CDP at a Deep Discount
mim-abracadabra.text: Battle-scarred {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin minted against Abracadabra cauldrons; reflexive peg, no modeled {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop, and a remaining user base too stubborn or leveraged to leave. Magic Internet Money has survived multiple cauldron exploits, a treasury-manager scandal, a governance token collapse, and a long history of violent peg excursions, which makes its continued existence less a triumph than a lab result. The collateral base still reads like a museum of DeFi exotica: yvDAI dominates, WBTC is material, and smaller yvWETH/WETH cauldrons keep the wrapper risk alive. The mechanism is reflexive rather than structural. Borrowers buy discounted MIM to repay debt, which only works when borrowers exist and care about their positions. June finally broke the pattern: MIM crashed through half a dollar in its worst depeg on record, Abracadabra's emergency response, including rate hikes, incentive pauses, and a token Curve-pool injection, failed to hold the line, and Pharos's multi-source feed now prices the token at a deep double-digit discount with the report card at F. MIM earned its cockroach reputation by surviving what killed everything else; this time the exterminator appears to be arithmetic.

usdp-paxos.title: The Credentialed Reference Implementation
usdp-paxos.text: Paxos's USDP is backed by very-low-risk reserves split across short-dated {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, overnight repos, and FDIC-insured cash, attested monthly by KPMG under Paxos's OCC National Trust Charter. Backing and economic control are the product's obvious strengths in the Safety Score V9 report card; the gap between those pillars and a genuinely elite overall grade lives in the exit pillar, because thin markets remain the asset's perennial soft spot. USDP has become less a growth product than a credentialed reference implementation. Paxos's real business is white-labeling stablecoin infrastructure for PayPal, Global Dollar Network, and formerly Binance. The depeg events on record read like thin-market artifacts rather than backing failure, but thin markets are still what holders have to trade through. The current package remains one of the cleaner compliance-to-reserves stories in the small-cap tier, with zero-fee {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} as the structural floor under a token almost nobody seems eager to hold.

usdd-tron-dao-reserve.title: Back to TRX-Heavy Backing
usdd-tron-dao-reserve.text: USDD has pivoted again: the reserve is once more dominated by TRX as CDP collateral, with a sliver of sTRX, alongside a Smart Allocator sleeve of DeFi strategies and a thin USDT PSM buffer, a return to the TRX-heavy {{term:algorithmic}}volatile-asset{{/term}} composition that defined USDD's earlier era. That is a striking backing profile for an asset that now sits at a D overall safety grade, dragged down by an F on the economic-control pillar and the structural fact that its dollar value rests on the most volatile single asset in the TRON orbit. The peg itself behaves better than the rest of the profile deserves, and the asset rarely strays from the calm end of the stress scale, but that surface stability has been bought across hundreds of brief deviations over the years. The {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} backstop remains the load-bearing piece: permissionless atomic swaps with zero fees and an immediate USDT exit lane give the exit pillar a redemption quality the surrounding reserve mix can't match. With Dominica jurisdiction and governance still set by fiat, USDD survives not on collateral merit but on the TRON ecosystem's captive demand and its founder's conviction that centralized control is a feature.

dola-inverse-finance.title: Rebuilt on FiRM, Concentrated in sUSDe
dola-inverse-finance.text: DOLA is Inverse Finance's CDP-style stablecoin minted via FiRM lending, with a USDS PSM as its peg floor. Inverse Finance's twin $24M exploits in 2022 left scars that became load-bearing, and the protocol genuinely rebuilt from near-zero credibility on the back of FiRM's fixed-rate lending markets generating organic borrower demand; circulation has recovered into nine figures. The C+ report card reflects a collateral base that has become anything but diversified: sUSDe now makes up north of 80% of the backing, a concentration that keeps the backing pillar pinned in C territory and effectively chains DOLA's fate to Ethena's synthetic dollar. The sDOLA {{term:yield-bearing}}yield{{/term}} remains the quiet attraction here, sourced from actual borrower interest rather than token emissions, and DEWS tends to hover near the cautious end of the stress scale rather than the calm one. DOLA survived exploits severe enough to end many protocols, but hundreds of brief sub-peg blips and a worst deviation that once approached total collapse remain the asterisk on every metric, and the {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}'s USDS backstop is real but thin against that history. DOLA is minted from overcollateralized {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style FiRM loans with {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} backstops.

sdola-inverse-finance.title: DOLA With an Exchange Rate
sdola-inverse-finance.text: sDOLA is the ERC-4626 wrapper around DOLA's savings account, which means the stablecoin risk is still DOLA and the extra product risk is the exchange-rate wrapper sitting on top. FiRM borrowing revenue is converted through the DBR-DOLA auction and compounded into a rising DOLA:sDOLA exchange rate, so the yield story is at least tied to borrower demand rather than a mystery emissions spreadsheet. The wrapper does not create new base DOLA supply, but holders still inherit DOLA's CDP collateral mix, governance scars, and any upstream stress in the parent peg. Cross-chain deployments on Base, Optimism, Arbitrum, and Berachain broaden access while keeping Ethereum as the source of truth, which is convenient until the bridge path becomes the part everyone suddenly remembers.

gusd-gemini.title: Pristine Reserves, Ghost Town Liquidity
gusd-gemini.text: GUSD is Gemini Trust's NYDFS-chartered dollar redeemable 1:1 against State Street/Western Alliance cash and short {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}. It has pristine compliance and almost no users. Gemini Dollar's reserve is impeccable: T-bills and cash at State Street and Western Alliance Bank, NYDFS trust charter, and zero {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} fees. The problem is that nobody uses it, and the v9 report card renders the split with unusual clarity: a B+ backing pillar and an economic-control pillar in the A range, but the exit pillar scrapes along at C-, dragging the overall grade to C+ because on-chain exit remains a mostly theoretical exercise. With circulating supply down more than 90% from its late-2022 peak, GUSD has become a regulatory trophy collecting dust. Its hundreds of brief price blips are the signature of an asset so thinly traded that any flow nudges the quote, with the sharpest excursions skewing negative even as the peg recovers each time. Gemini built the compliance-first stablecoin that regulators asked for, and the market responded with a collective shrug.

sources.label: DefiLlama: Gemini Dollar circulating supply history

alusd-alchemix.title: Self-Repaying Dollar
alusd-alchemix.text: alUSD is Alchemix's self-repaying {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin: deposit DAI, USDC, or USDT into Yearn and Aave yield strategies, borrow up to roughly 50% against it, and let the yield slowly erase your debt with no interest and no {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} risk. The mechanism remains DeFi's most patient financial product, and the Transmuter still backstops 1:1 {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} on a queue that settles over days. But the elegance has a price the report card spells out plainly: an overall F, driven by a peg record so poor that the v9 peg multiplier does most of the damage; self-repaying loans strip out the debt-repayment urgency that normally generates buying pressure to defend the peg. The peg has logged brief deviations by the hundreds across its history and rarely sits comfortably at the calm end of the stress scale, so holders are effectively trading away peg discipline for the no-liquidation feature. Exit routes have thinned to a D-grade pillar, and even backing is held back by stale evidence: no current reserve composition on file, leaving economic control at a respectable B- as the only part of this battle-tested architecture v9 still likes. A stress-prone instrument that only makes sense if you value never being liquidated above all else.

susd-synthetix.title: Retired Below Par
susd-synthetix.text: Synthetix's sUSD is no longer the simple SNX debt-pool dollar older DeFi muscle memory remembers. The current reserve story is split across legacy SNX exposure, V3 USDC/stataUSDC collateral, ETH/LST collateral, and protocol treasury or SLP-vault activity, which is a long way of saying the peg now depends on governance executing a cleanup plan. Pharos flags the prolonged discount because this is not a theoretical stress test; the token has been living below its target while the V3 transition and basis-trade restoration plan try to rebuild demand. The mint path is governed through Synthetix admin control rather than immutable borrower autonomy, so holders are underwriting both collateral volatility and political patience. In June the roadmap ran out: governance passed SIP-423, retiring sUSD outright. The contract is frozen. Holders are compensated at four SNX per sUSD on a year's lock and a year's vest. Pharos no longer gets a continuous price read on what was DeFi's original synthetic dollar. Eight years of peg engineering ends not with a bang but with a conversion schedule.

ousd-origin-protocol.title: The Passive Yield Play
ousd-origin-protocol.text: Yield-bearing rebasing USDC wrapper that deploys deposits into Morpho and Curve strategies; yield attributable to non-opted balances is redirected to opted-in holders, with one of the stronger permissionless redemption backstops in the yield-bearing set. Origin Dollar is fully backed by USDC routed through Morpho/Yearn vault exposure and Curve {{term:amo}}AMO{{/term}} liquidity, {{term:yield-bearing}}rebasing daily{{/term}} so opted-in balances grow without staking or locking. Smart contracts must explicitly opt in to receive yield, so OUSD sitting in non-opted AMM pools transfers its attributable return to opted-in balances. Permissionless atomic stablecoin {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} at a small fee provides a structural floor that many depeg blips have tested but not broken. The exotic collateral quality and wrapper governance classification reflect what OUSD actually is: a USDC yield strategy with a rebasing token wrapper, not an independent stablecoin with its own reserve management. It is a well-engineered product for the small cohort that wants DeFi yield without the DeFi homework, and the cohort remains tellingly small.

cusd-celo.title: Stablecoins All the Way Down
cusd-celo.text: USDm is Mento's oracle-priced USD stablecoin on Celo, mostly backed by other stablecoins with a CELO wildcard. Mento Dollar (USDm, formerly cUSD) is an exercise in recursive stablecoin nesting: roughly four-fifths of the reserve is other people's stablecoins: AUSD and sUSDS are the largest slices, with USDT, EURC, and USDC layered on top, meaning the majority of USDm's backing is itself backed elsewhere, each layer with its own dependency chain and failure modes. A long tail of mostly minor depeg events and a worst drawdown past 11% are hard numbers to look past, and the report card has slid to a D: not because the backing is weak (that pillar holds a respectable B-) but because the exit pillar sits at F: {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} runs through Mento reserve swaps rather than fiat off-ramps, and the on-chain depth behind those swaps is thin. The thesis remains phone-number wallets in places like Nairobi, not DeFi composability on Ethereum. The CELO allocation, roughly a sixth of the reserve, is the wildcard in an otherwise stablecoin-heavy book: the one asset that can crater in a downturn precisely when a thin {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} buffer matters most.

eurc-circle.title: MiCA's Compliance Moat
eurc-circle.text: Circle's EURC is the regulatory standard-bearer for euro stablecoins: an ACPR-licensed EMI under MiCA, {{term:attestation}}Deloitte-examined{{/term}} monthly, and now native on roughly a dozen chains rather than the handful it launched with. The June 30 examination shows a reserve that is entirely cash at regulated financial institutions: no securities whatsoever, which is defensible for a euro float and a reminder that EURC's real counterparty is a set of banks Circle declines to name, with only a sliver of the balance sitting where the feed marks the institution as systemically important. Re-anchoring the curated composition to that examination cost the card nothing: the live rows still bind, backing held, and exit liquidity, the strongest thing here, never wobbled. The moat stopped being theoretical when MiCA's transitional window closed and USDT liquidity on licensed European venues collapsed, leaving Circle's pair as most of what remains on regulated shelves. EURC is the largest euro stablecoin by a wide margin and still a rounding error against USDC: a float that thin registers tremors a deeper pool would never feel, even when the stress panel reads quiet.

eurs-stasis.title: Reserves Without a Market Path
eurs-stasis.text: EURS is STASIS's euro stablecoin redeemable 1:1 against EU bank balances: the original euro stablecoin, launched in 2018, now the cautionary tale of the category it created. The static file still reads respectable: Malta MFSA context and liquid euro balances at licensed European institutions including central-bank accounts, though reserve assurance has thinned to a self-published daily transparency statement rather than independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}. The live report card fails in a specific way: backing and economic control both hold C+ territory, while the peg fails outright and the exit pillar scores an actual zero: the reserves may exist, but the market path back to par does not. That is not an abstraction: through early 2026 EURS swung violently on both sides of its euro peg, from a February low near $0.63 to an April spike past $1.20 in a single day, the kind of round trips that pile up in Pharos's dozens of logged depeg events and keep the stress band elevated. The verdict has hardened: pristine {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and a transparency page can keep a product alive, but with no depth to exit into, the quote is whatever the last thin trade says it is.

sources.label: Blockchain Magazine on the April 2026 EURS depeg swing

ceur-celo.title: The Other Mento Euro
ceur-celo.text: EURm is Mento's oracle-priced EUR stablecoin on Celo, sharing the Mento reserve at ~136% overcollateralization. Mento Euro (EURm, formerly CEUR) shares the same Mento reserve as Mento Dollar: 56% sUSDS, 22% EURC, 12% CELO, and smaller positions in various stablecoins and ETH, at approximately 136% {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}}, stabilized via the BiPoolManager virtual AMM with oracle-enforced EUR rates. As a crypto-backed coin, EURm inherits both the strengths (on-chain transparency, overcollateralization) and weaknesses (crypto collateral volatility, thin secondary markets) of the Mento system. Deployed on Celo (now an Ethereum L2) with real-time on-chain reserve verification, EURm exists primarily to serve Celo's vision of region-specific stablecoins for mobile payments rather than DeFi composability. In the euro stablecoin race dominated by Circle's EURC and MiCA-licensed competitors, EURm's niche is geographic rather than regulatory. {{term:redemption}}Redemption{{/term}} runs through Mento reserve swaps rather than fiat off-ramps.

fpi-frax.title: CPI on a Blockchain
fpi-frax.text: FPI is Frax's CPI-tracking stablecoin backed by FRAX reserves and {{term:amo}}AMO{{/term}}-generated yield: an inflation derivative with single-issuer dependency. Frax Price Index tracks purchasing power rather than a dollar, with a {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} price that ratchets upward every second at the trailing 12-month CPI-U rate via Chainlink oracle. That makes it both a stablecoin and an inflation derivative, backed entirely by FRAX reserves and AMO yield: exactly the recursive dependency the report card flags as the soft spot, with backing the weakest of the three pillars: FPI's collateral quality is only as good as FRAX itself, and the chain inherits every flaw upstream carries. The rest of the card has firmed up to a B- overall, exit and economic control both holding in B territory, which leaves the quieter problem: a modest float that keeps FPI more curiosity than market, however sound the machinery underneath. A clever idea that now scores better than it trades: the inflation hedge works, but almost nobody is holding it.

uusd-youves.title: The Zero-Score Tezos Dollar
uusd-youves.text: Youves's uUSD is a Tezos {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} backed by XTZ, tzBTC, USDt, and SIRS LP tokens, and it still holds the only distinction worse than an F grade: a safety score of literally zero, the absolute floor of the Pharos scale. The peg failure is permanent and active. It has well over a thousand recorded depeg events, zero DEX pools, no backstop route, and no market mechanism left to enforce parity on a Tezos ecosystem that emptied out beneath it. The one dark joke in the report card is a mid-tier backing pillar: the {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} vault math still technically works, which counts for little when exit and control sit at the floor. And the rigor mortis has finally broken. Circulating value has roughly halved from the ~$11.5M plateau it held into early July, less stability now than slow-motion dismantling as remaining vault owners unwind what markets no longer price. The uUSD story remains a cautionary tale about chain risk: sound {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} mechanics are worthless when the entire ecosystem around them goes dark.

lisusd-lista.title: BNB Chain's CDP Bet
lisusd-lista.text: BNB Chain CDP backed mostly by BNB-ecosystem assets (BNB, slisBNB, BETH, BTCB) with a PSM against USDT/USDC/FDUSD; 387 depeg events on the record. Lista DAO's lisUSD transplants the MakerDAO CDP playbook to BNB Chain with a collateral mix that is 60% BNB ecosystem assets: 35% native BNB and 25% slisBNB (Lista's own LST), plus 15% Binance-wrapped ETH and 10% BTCB, with a PSM accepting USDT, USDC, and FDUSD for peg stability. The 387 depeg events including one that cratered nearly 6,000 basis points below peg make lisUSD one of the most frequently depegged CDPs at scale, though the 85-rated PSM backstop with permissionless atomic settlement provides the structural floor. Deployed only on BSC with alt-LST collateral quality and no jurisdiction or proof of reserves disclosed, lisUSD's safety profile depends entirely on BNB's price stability and the PSM's capacity to absorb redemption pressure. Whether lisUSD can grow beyond Binance-subsidized adoption remains the central question for a CDP whose collateral and distribution both flow through a single ecosystem. The model is a standard {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} with BNB-heavy {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}}, LST-collateral {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} risk, and a permissionless atomic {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} as the peg floor.

eure-monerium.title: SEPA Native, DeFi Adopted
eure-monerium.text: EURE is Monerium's MiCA-regulated euro e-money; SEPA-native mint and burn, safeguarded mostly in an LVNAV fund plus bank deposits. Monerium's EURe is what happens when an Icelandic EMI license meets actual product-market fit: SEPA-to-IBAN integration that lets users move between euros and on-chain tokens without the friction that plagues most stablecoin on-ramps, with the bulk of reserves safeguarded in State Street's AAA-rated EUR LVNAV {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}} and the rest in deposits at Arion and LHV, with weights Monerium does not publish. That disclosure gap is what holds the overall grade down in the C range: the safeguarding structure reads like the top tier's on paper, but the backing pillar grades what is proven, and self-reported reserves with public attestations still 'being prepared' cannot outscore their paperwork. Distribution is the counterweight: a deployment sprawling from Ethereum and its L2s to Gnosis, Polygon, Cosmos rails, and Algorand, though DEX depth still tilts toward a couple of dominant pools, a mismatch the peg record documents in a string of brief wobbles. Iceland's FSA may lack the brand cachet of France's ACPR. Burning EURe and crediting EUR via SEPA through {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} remains the one exit that never depends on pool depth. The real gap to the top tier is simpler: EURC shows its reserves monthly to a Big Four examiner, and Monerium still asks you to take its word.

eusd-electronic-usd.title: Lending Basket With First-Loss Risk
eusd-electronic-usd.text: eUSD is a Reserve Protocol RToken wrapping Compound and Aave USDC/USDT lending positions in DeFi, with RSR stakers absorbing first-loss: a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} basket whose machinery works better than its report card. Electronic USD combines Compound V3 USDC, Aave V3 USDC, and Compound V3 USDT in Reserve Protocol's permissionless basket {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanism, with RSR stakers absorbing the first-loss risk. The peg holds A-grade tightness, the coin rarely strays from the calm end of the stress scale, and atomic permissionless redemption keeps the exit pillar respectable; the hundreds of historical depeg blips are real but largely ancient, the worst a roughly 13% gash in earlier days. So why does the overall grade sit down at D? Economic control fails outright because multisig-held mint authority governs a wrapper that leans entirely on Aave, Compound, and the USDC/USDT underneath. V9 treats that as a first-class risk rather than a footnote. Backing and exit earn only C+ marks once those dependencies are priced in. Supply has been essentially flat in the low tens of millions for months, neither growing nor contracting, which is either stability or irrelevance depending on your perspective.

crvusd-curve.title: LLAMMA on Custodial Bitcoin
crvusd-curve.text: crvUSD is Curve's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin with LLAMMA soft-liquidation and deep DEX liquidity, but most collateral is custodial WBTC/cbBTC. When the protocol that dominates stablecoin DEX routing launches its own stablecoin, the design had better be interesting. LLAMMA replaces cliff-edge {{term:liquidation}}liquidations{{/term}} with gradual rebalancing through price bands. The report card remains solid rather than elite because the collateral story contains a structural contradiction: Bitcoin collateral running through BitGo and Coinbase introduces exactly the centralized {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} dependencies crypto-native collateral was supposed to avoid. PegKeeper pools paired with USDC, USDT, PYUSD, frxUSD, and GHO provide active peg machinery, while scrvUSD creates a yield feedback loop where stress can pull buyers back in. Curve still gives crvUSD the deepest on-chain liquidity footprint among CDP dollars, but even home-field advantage cannot fully insulate a crypto-backed stablecoin from the deleveraging cycles that govern its borrowers.

gho-aave.title: DeFi's Most Liquid Dollar
gho-aave.text: GHO is Aave's decentralized dollar minted by borrowing against Aave collateral: a diversified {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} dollar drawn from the protocol's battle-tested pools. The B overall grade splits cleanly across the V9 pillars. Exit is near-flawless because a deeply distributed DEX footprint plus {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}-style GSM redemption make it about as clean as on-chain exits get, while backing lags at the bottom of the report card, because the collateral is whatever mixed crypto Aave's risk machinery accepts, and economic control prices the governance that steers it all. The hundreds of brief sub-peg blips are scars from GHO's rocky early months; the peg has long since settled toward the calm end of the stress scale. Governance took its live test when the Aave Chan Initiative, the delegate shop that shepherded GHO's early growth, and core developer BGD Labs both walked away amid a DAO rift, yet the dollar barely flinched: Aave V4 shipped on Ethereum mainnet this spring with its unified-liquidity hub-and-spoke architecture, the sGHO savings vault launched at a fixed rate in April, and a governance proposal would push sGHO cross-chain starting with Arbitrum. Circulation has kept climbing toward the three-quarter-billion mark, cementing GHO as one of the largest CDP-style dollars outside Sky's orbit. Aave proved a lending protocol can birth a credible dollar if it iterates in public; the backing pillar's C+ is the bill for letting that dollar lean on the whole lending book.

sources.label: Aave V4 is Live on Ethereum

fdusd-first-digital.title: Binance's Current Favorite
fdusd-first-digital.text: FDUSD is a BVI-issued dollar stablecoin backed by short-dated {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} and cash, custodied by First Digital Trust, and the custodian risk stopped being abstract in April 2025. First Digital USD rose to prominence as Binance's preferred stablecoin after BUSD's regulatory demise, and the lineage worry crystallized when Justin Sun publicly claimed the {{term:custody}}custodian{{/term}} was insolvent: FDUSD broke to $0.87 within hours before recovering, and First Digital answered with a Hong Kong defamation suit seeking retractions and damages: a peg defended in court filings as much as in redemption windows. The reserves themselves remain conventional: overwhelmingly short-dated T-bills and cash, {{term:attestation}}attested{{/term}} monthly, most recently by Hong Kong's AOGB for end-June 2026, but the {{grade}} overall grade shows where Pharos sees the weakness: backing and exit both sit in D territory, less about what is in the reserves than who vouches for and custodies them, while the peg holds A-grade tightness and the depeg history reads as brief episodes rather than chronic drift. Deployed across six chains including Sui, TON, and Solana, the distribution still follows Binance's ecosystem preferences more than organic DeFi demand. FDUSD's fate remains a single-dependency story: Binance's endorsement made it, one custodian tweet-storm nearly unmade it, and Binance's pivot to another favorite could finish the job.

sources.label: CoinDesk: First Digital Trust serves Justin Sun with defamation claim
BeInCrypto: FDUSD depegs to $0.87 after Justin Sun insolvency claims

pyusd-paypal.title: The Respectable Waiting Room
pyusd-paypal.text: PayPal's KPMG-examined PYUSD still carries one of the cleanest reserve profiles Pharos tracks: overnight {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} reverse repos with a cash sleeve underneath, held at Paxos under an OCC national trust charter, and the backing pillar has not moved an inch. What moved is Pharos. The 9.12 incident-decay ladder now prices a resolved mint incident as a full posture class rather than a footnote, so the October 2025 episode in which a Paxos internal transfer conjured roughly $300 trillion of PYUSD before burning it the same day caps the economic-control pillar and drags an A-grade backing profile down to a B- overall. The cap is scheduled rather than permanent: it relaxes in October 2027 and again in October 2029, by which point Paxos's seasoned-issuer credit should restore the old grade. The recorded limitation is worth stating plainly: the ladder measures how long ago an incident happened, not how bad it was, so a same-day-reversed operational error draws the same cap as an exploit that left real bad debt behind. Adoption remains the other open question: Mastercard's settlement expansion put Paxos rails into card back-office plumbing, but the float has shrunk by roughly a third from its March peak, which reads more like crypto-native capital parking rotating out than PayPal's retail network transacting on-chain.

sources.label: Cryptonomist: PYUSD supply near $2.7B in early August 2026, down from $4B+ in March

gyen-gyen.title: Regulated in the Wrong Country
gyen-gyen.text: GYEN is GMO Trust's NYDFS-chartered yen stablecoin backed by FDIC cash and {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}. It has pristine custody, near-zero on-chain usage, and now an orderly wind-down notice. It holds the distinction of being one of the most heavily regulated JPY stablecoins in existence, though the regulator is New York rather than Tokyo. GMO Trust's charter, monthly Network Firm {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}}, and very-low-risk reserve model would be impressive if the market still cared. The problem is the secondary market: thin DEX liquidity and a long depeg history make GYEN trade less like a stablecoin and more like a neglected FX derivative. The 2021 depeg litigation and 2026 wind-down notice turn the dashboard's failing profile into a verdict rather than a warning. This is pristine {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} architecture wrapped around a token whose main remaining use case is redemption before the lights go out.

usdy-ondo-finance.title: Clean Treasuries, Multi-Day Exit
usdy-ondo-finance.text: Ondo's USDY carries a {{grade}} safety grade, and the spread of its pillars explains the discount better than any headline figure. The backing is about as clean as tokenized {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} exposure gets on paper. It includes short-term U.S. Treasuries, iShares short Treasury ETF shares, and bank demand deposits, with daily NAV {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} from Ankura Trust. Yet the backing pillar only manages a C-, because v9 grades the mechanism wrapped around the assets, not just their quality on paper. The exit pillar grades D on weak on-chain liquidity and a multi-day {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} window through the BVI-domiciled, issuer-controlled structure, despite a footprint spanning roughly a dozen networks from Ethereum and Solana through Cosmos chains like Noble and Mantra, while economic control at B- is, a little ironically, the strongest thing on the card. The peg itself stays unremarkable, with no depeg events on record and nothing flagging stress. That is the point of a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} NAV token that accrues value rather than chasing a hard dollar. USDY remains a clean way to hold American government debt for the non-U.S. investors that American regulators won't let buy it directly; the grade simply prices in that you're trusting Ondo's plumbing, not a market, to get your money back.

cadc-cad-coin.title: Backed by Scanned Bank Letters
cadc-cad-coin.text: CADC has been the on-chain loonie since 2021, with FINTRAC registration as an MSB under the Loon brand, 1:1 redemption against CAD held in trust at ATB Financial, and deployment across six chains including Solana. Its reach is broader than most local-currency stablecoins despite modest circulation. The regulatory waiting game it was built for is over: Canada's Stablecoin Act received royal assent in March 2026 as part of Bill C-15, naming the Bank of Canada as supervisor of stablecoin issuers, though the operative provisions await regulations expected to run into 2027. That timeline cuts both ways for a first mover, because Pharos's data shows the compliance story is thinner than the branding: reserve transparency amounts to monthly scanned bank-confirmation letters with no accountant's opinion and no reconciliation against circulating supply, exit liquidity is close to nonexistent, and the peg has logged dozens of deviation events: a failing overall report card despite solid economic-control marks. {{term:redemption}}Redemption{{/term}} 1:1 against trust-held CAD remains the design; the registry the Bank of Canada is about to open will decide whether the design is enough. Being first to a regulated market only pays if you can pass the exam you waited for.

sources.label: DLA Piper: Canada enacts stablecoin framework in Bill C-15 (April 2026)

cadd-cad-digital.title: Canada's Institutional CAD Rail
cadd-cad-digital.text: CADD launched in May 2026 as Canada's first CAD stablecoin issued by a regulated financial institution, Tetra Trust, under Alberta's Loan and Trust Corporations Act, with a backer roster (Shopify, National Bank of Canada, ATB Financial, Wealthsimple) that reads like a who's-who of Canadian fintech. It is now fully live on Pharos rather than coverage-pending, and the data is unusually clean for a long-tail fiat coin: a spotless peg record so far, and a backing pillar supported by monthly Baker Tilly reasonable-assurance {{term:attestation}}examinations{{/term}} that fully reconcile reserves against token liabilities: a transparency baseline most billion-dollar issuers do not meet. The catch is scale: circulation remains a rounding error next to that backer roster, and the exit pillar grades poorly because an institutional settlement rail has little use for DEX pools until institutions actually settle on it. With the Stablecoin Act now assented and the Bank of Canada assuming supervision, CADD's bet is that compliant infrastructure built before the rules arrive becomes the default once they do. The rail is impeccable; the traffic is still theoretical.

sources.label: Business Wire: Tetra Digital Group launches CADD (May 2026)

usde-ethena.title: The Basis Trade, Tokenized
usde-ethena.text: Ethena's USDe is still the tokenized basis trade, but the current reserve mix is more conservative and more complicated than the original pitch: roughly three quarters liquid stablecoins, about 16% BTC delta-neutral exposure, and about 8% ETH or LST delta-neutral exposure. The liquid-stable sleeve leans heavily on USDtb and therefore BlackRock BUIDL, while the hedged crypto sleeve still depends on off-exchange custody and CEX perpetual markets through venues such as Binance, Bybit, and OKX. Under Safety Score v9 the old contradiction has softened into a straight B, with the exit pillar now the standout in A territory: a flawless peg record, solid backing, and an economic-control pillar that passes now that scoring measures how mint, oracle, and bridge authority are actually bounded rather than ideological decentralization. That spread is worth reading carefully: real-time transparency from Ethena's dashboard helps even as the slower custodian-attestation trail runs months behind it, but neither turns CEX custody, backend-signed mint flows, or USDtb-to-BUIDL dependency into neutral facts. It means the machinery is well-run machinery. The institutional surface area keeps growing regardless. Robinhood's new chain launched with USDe as a primary collateral asset in its Earn program, curated by Steakhouse Financial, and the deployment map has since stretched to Avalanche and Monad. USDe's trick is making a risky institutional trade look calm at the token level; the dashboard's job is to keep pointing at the machinery underneath.

aeur-anchored-coins.title: Death of a Swiss Euro
aeur-anchored-coins.text: AEUR is Anchored Coins' centralized euro stablecoin, backed by euro reserves at Swissquote Bank SA, but the issuer is in a regulated wind-down with no new issuance. The FlowBank bankruptcy exposure that once complicated the backing has been resolved through that consolidation, yet the operating posture is permanent: MiCAR-era requirements leave a Swiss issuer no obvious reactivation path. Binance, the venue that once gave AEUR its reason to exist, has now completed the unwind, delisting the final spot pair at the end of July 2026 and, from mid-August, switching off withdrawals and auto-converting remaining balances to euros at 1:1. This was less a delisting than an escorted exit. Thin DEX trading and a large minimum for direct issuer {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} make the peg less something a market can repair than a balance sheet the issuer can settle. The reserves may be intact, but when your largest venue converts holders out whether they ask or not, the product is past hospice care. Only an estate sale remains.

sources.label: Binance: Notice Regarding the Removal of AEUR and Conversion of AEUR to EUR

buck-bucket-protocol.title: Sui's CDP Experiment
buck-bucket-protocol.text: BUCK is Bucket Protocol's {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} Sui-native dollar stablecoin minted from SUI, BTC, ETH, and LSTs through {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} vaults with {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} stablecoin swaps. Bucket Protocol brings the MakerDAO playbook to Sui: deposit SUI, USDC/USDT via PSM, wrapped BTC, or ETH/LSTs, mint BUCK at zero interest, get liquidated at 110% collateral ratio. The strong redemption backstop, direct BUCK {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for collateral, earns the exit pillar a passing mark and provides a real structural floor, but hundreds of depeg events, including one that cratered some 7,500 basis points below peg, reveal what happens when the primary collateral is a volatile L1 token. The overall F grade, though, is pinned in place by something more specific: a binding critical cap for a weak oracle branch: v9's way of saying the control topology of the price feeds BUCK depends on is opaque, and a CDP that liquidates at 110% is only as honest as the oracle nobody can inspect. The PSM module accepting USDC and USDT remains a polite way of saying the decentralized stablecoin ultimately leans on centralized ones when it matters, and the currently placid stress reading sits oddly on a product whose history includes some of the most severe depegs of any surviving CDP.

vchf-vnx.title: VNX Liechtenstein Franc Token
vchf-vnx.text: VNX's VCHF is a CHF-redeemable stablecoin operating under Liechtenstein's TVTG Blockchain Act with FMA oversight. Its reserve reports establish aggregate CHF-value coverage held in bank and/or securities custody accounts, but do not disclose the holdings or category split: regulated is not the same thing as fully legible. Direct issuer {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and broad deployment infrastructure give the token more operational scaffolding than its thin on-chain trading demand appears to require. That makes VCHF a competent niche instrument, but not a self-sustaining CHF DeFi market. The remaining issue is whether a regulated franc rail finds a use case before its distribution footprint becomes an expensive museum exhibit.

veur-vnx.title: Terminated as Unpriceable
veur-vnx.text: VNX's euro token spread itself across a dozen chains under Liechtenstein FMA Blockchain Act licensing, and the market mostly declined to move in. The float stayed a rounding error beside EURC while trading thinned past the point where a dependable price could be established at all. Pharos terminated VEUR tracking on 2026-07-19 as an unpriceable asset: without a reliable market price path, peg, liquidity, and safety scoring all become fiction, so the listing was removed outright rather than frozen or sent to the cemetery. Nothing in the exit impugns the reserve substance. Fiat {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, formal {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and same-day issuer {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for KYC customers were real. Regulated plumbing without market gravity is infrastructure without traffic. MiCA-era competition from bank-grade euro issuers made the FMA license second-tier at precisely the moment VEUR needed distribution most. The multi-chain footprint outlived the market that was supposed to fill it.

audd-novatti.title: Australia's Compliance Play
audd-novatti.text: AUDD is what happens when a listed fintech builds a stablecoin the way regulators wish everyone would: AUD cash at Australian deposit-taking institutions, an AFSL from ASIC, monthly William Buck procedures, and a seat in the Reserve Bank's Project Acacia pilot. Until the July reserve report landed, that credential stack was worth surprisingly little to the score, because the composition on file had aged past the 31-day freshness window and the card sat under a ceiling for having no admissible reserve composition at all. The report fixed that by arriving on time. A modest cash reserve split between a Westpac bare trust and Banking Circle agreed without exception against on-chain supply across eight networks. The backing pillar climbed into B territory, though the overall card still sits at C with a thin exit pillar doing the holding back. The honest reading is that AUDD's evidence became timely, while the underlying product did not change. The same dating rule had that effect on several commodity and regional tokens this cycle. Worth keeping in view: William Buck's engagement is agreed-upon procedures that expressly declines to express an opinion. AUDD's constraint is whether Australia's on-chain economy grows large enough to want a domestic dollar.

sources.label: William Buck: AUDD Agreed-Upon Procedures Report, July 2026

cgusd-cygnus-finance.title: Base's Treasury Wrapper
cgusd-cygnus-finance.text: cgUSD is Cygnus Finance's daily-rebasing T-bill dollar on Base; NAV-vs-price arbitrage friction has produced a long tail of depeg events. The reserve model is clean on paper: 80% off-chain {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, 15% on-chain USDC/USDT, and accrued interest, with a Transmuter giving holders instant 1:1 conversion to USDC when it has capacity. The depeg history tells a different story than the treasury-wrapper pitch, because the gap between off-chain NAV and on-chain price creates arbitrage friction the rebase mechanism cannot fully erase. Institutional-unregulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} with no robust published proof path leaves the trust assumptions sitting mostly with the Cygnus team. Base-only deployment is pragmatic for a USDC-heavy product, but the multi-day settlement window outside the Transmuter means cgUSD's convenience premium is narrower than the wrapper makes it look. The reserve is an {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} basket; the exit experience is still very much a DeFi product.

fxusd-f-x-protocol.title: Leverage as a Peg Mechanism
fxusd-f-x-protocol.text: fxUSD is f(x) Protocol's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-minted dollar {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} by WBTC and wstETH, with a Stability Pool arbitraging Curve to defend the peg. f(x) Protocol turns leveraged long positions into peg defense: xPOSITION NFTs represent looped exposure to a majority-WBTC collateral mix, while fxUSD holders get the stable side of the trade. The design has outgrown its niche; circulation has more than tripled since spring into the mid-eight figures, and the B overall grade holds, with backing now the strongest of its three pillars even as WBTC's BitGo/Coinbase custody sits awkwardly inside a nominally decentralized machine. It earns its keep through an atomic {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop and a Stability Pool that actively arbitrages the USDC/fxUSD Curve pool, while dozens of brief depeg blips show the mechanism wobbles but recovers. The exit pillar is the laggard: DEX liquidity remains concentrated enough that one pool failure would gut exit capacity. A clever design that works until vol overwhelms the leverage.

usdb-blast.title: Post-Airdrop Decay
usdb-blast.text: USDB's reserve is quality stablecoin collateral routed through MakerDAO DSR, but the product is stranded on a chain the market stopped caring about post-airdrop. The current metadata models the backing through Blast's DAI yield manager, which is less exotic than the surrounding ecosystem branding would suggest. The long depeg history tells the story of a rebasing stablecoin on an island where liquidity and attention both thinned after incentives faded. Governance-set yield barely registers against the cost of holding a chain-native wrapper with no issuer-style {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop. The safety profile is dragged down by Blast-only deployment and fallback-class secondary liquidity, even though the underlying collateral would look respectable in a more liquid wrapper. USDB is a technically competent product stuck in a room where the party ended and the lights are still on.

buidl-blackrock.title: The Stablecoin's Stablecoin
buidl-blackrock.text: BUIDL is BlackRock's tokenized institutional {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}}, NAV-pegged to $1 and backed by U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}}, repos, and cash custodied by BNY Mellon. It has become the largest tokenized money market fund and the asset that a growing list of stablecoins (USDe, USDtb, frxUSD, USD0, CASH) hold in their own reserves rather than managing T-bill {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} directly. Its C+ report card is a reminder that Pharos measures structural risk, not brand prestige: top-tier institutional custody at BNY Mellon and a reserve mix of very-low-risk assets earn a B+ backing pillar, but the exit pillar grades D: zero DEX liquidity and Reg D access restrictions confine BUIDL to a world invisible to retail, where exit means a transfer agent, not a market. The roughly 3.5% NAV-appreciation yield net of 20 bps fees is T-bill rate pass-through, unremarkable on its own but compelling when you consider it comes with BlackRock counterparty risk rather than crypto-native smart contract risk. Eight chain deployments via Securitize are expanding the footprint, but BUIDL's true significance is infrastructural. It is the infrastructure layer where TradFi yield enters crypto's reserve stacks, not an asset most humans will ever hold directly.

btcusd-btcfi.title: Bitcoin's CDP Outpost
btcusd-btcfi.text: BtcUSD is BTCfi's {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} USD stablecoin minted from BTC variants through Liquity-style {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} vaults. The backing is all Bitcoin exposure in various wrapped or native forms: WBTC, BTCB, cbBTC, and BTC, which gives holders hard-money aesthetics plus every {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} assumption those wrappers drag along. Its long depeg history makes it one of the noisier CDPs per unit of market relevance, even if the live stress signal is not currently screaming. Deployed on Base and Bifrost with no modeled {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop, the practical exit route is secondary-market liquidity on chains the broader DeFi market does not heavily visit. The question remains whether BTC holders will trust yet another wrapping layer when established CDPs already accept wrapped Bitcoin with better liquidity and peg infrastructure.

usbd-bima.title: BTC Collateral, CDP Ambitions
usbd-bima.text: USBD is a Liquity-style BTC-LST {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin whose 150% mechanics are undermined by high-risk wrapper collateral and a barely tested secondary market. Bima puts Bitcoin liquid staking and restaking derivatives into overcollateralized vaults, with permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for BTC-denominated collateral and a {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} for near-1:1 stablecoin swaps. The live grade has slipped from the earlier flattering read because the peg can look calm when almost nobody is trading it. The collateral is not plain BTC but a chain of wrappers and restaking derivatives where each layer adds {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} and {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} assumptions the Liquity mechanics were designed to avoid. The permissionless backstop is structurally strong on paper; with no meaningful secondary market, the practical exit remains an open question rather than a settled one.

doc-money-on-chain.title: Bitcoin, Not Bank Deposits
doc-money-on-chain.text: DOC is Money On Chain's rBTC-collateralized USD stablecoin on Rootstock; small, but proof Bitcoin-collateralized dollars are alive outside Ethereum. Dollar on Chain is one of the cleaner hard-money stablecoin designs in the tracked set: no bank reserve story, no fiat {{term:custody}}custodian{{/term}}, just rBTC locked inside Money On Chain and a protocol that lets holders move back into Bitcoin-sidechain collateral when they want out. That simplicity cuts both ways. DOC's reserve logic is easier to trust than most small fiat tokens, but its market depth, chain reach, and surrounding infrastructure are far thinner than mainstream dollar stablecoins. With a circulating float in the low single-digit millions, DOC matters less as a payments network than as proof that Bitcoin-collateralized dollars are still alive outside Ethereum's orbit. Mechanically DOC is a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} against rBTC with {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for rBTC.

usdrif-rif.title: The RIF-Collateralized Dollar
usdrif-rif.text: USDRIF is a Rootstock {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin minted against RIF token collateral. It is onchain and transparent, but reserve quality is weak relative to BTC-backed alternatives. RIF US Dollar pushes the Rootstock stablecoin experiment further out on the risk curve than DOC: the peg is maintained with RIF collateral rather than Bitcoin collateral, which keeps everything onchain and transparent while making the reserve much weaker in quality. The protocol docs support minting and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} through {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} positions exposed to {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} risk, but the structure is still niche: small, volatile-collateral-backed, and dependent on a market that has never reached real scale. That makes USDRIF worth tracking as a live Rootstock stablecoin, not as a high-confidence safe haven.

isc-international-stable-currency.title: The Anti-Dollar Experiment
isc-international-stable-currency.text: ISC deliberately rejects the dollar peg and tries to stabilize purchasing power through a basket split across gold, investment-grade bonds, short-term T-bills, equities, and cash. That makes it one of the more intellectually honest uses of the word stable: nominal price can drift upward because the target is a basket, not one dollar frozen in amber. The catch is equally direct: Solana-only issuance, institutional-unregulated custody, and a retained freeze authority make the control surface much less elegant than the monetary philosophy. Pharos treats it as a NAV-style RWA token, useful as an inflation argument and awkward as everyday settlement. Being philosophically right is not the same thing as being liquid, which is the part every flatcoin eventually has to learn.

usd0-usual.title: Six Wrappers Deep
usd0-usual.text: USD0 is an RWA-backed dollar layered across USYC, M0's M, and Ethena's USDtb. Each is held through Usual's own wrapper contracts, with USDC as the deposit gateway. Every supposedly boring {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} component arrives with another issuer's operating model and counterparty chain attached. That compounding is exactly what the report card prices in: the backing pillar gets marked down through the wrapper stack, and economic control fails outright on centralized, multisig-governed admin keys, which is why the overall grade stays in the basement despite excellent peg behavior. The genuine structural strength is exit: the permissionless {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path through DaoCollateral earns an A- pillar, so holders can leave at will even when secondary markets wobble, as dozens of small recorded depeg blips show they periodically do. The market still remembers the USD0++ episode, which proved that clever tokenomics can complicate even a diversified reserve base. France-domiciled, RWA-backed, and architecturally ambitious, USD0 remains a bet that several low-risk parts do not add up to one meaningfully riskier whole. The scorecard keeps declining to take that bet.

usr-resolv.title: Frozen at Sixteen Cents
usr-resolv.text: Resolv's USR was a {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} synthetic dollar with an RLP insurance layer; it collapsed in 2026 after an EOA-minter exploit produced 80M unbacked tokens and depegged the asset, and the token was frozen. Resolv's USR was a {{term:basis-trade}}basis trade{{/term}}-driven synthetic dollar whose RLP insurance layer was supposed to absorb negative {{term:funding-rate}}funding rate{{/term}} pressure and protect USR holders until an EOA-minter exploit produced 80M unbacked tokens and shattered the peg. By the time of the freeze, USR had collapsed to $0.164, an 83.6% deviation from its dollar target. The permanent record shows 25 depeg events, including a worst of 9,025 basis points. Supply was volatile in the months leading up to the failure, swinging from $17.5M to $28.4M to $22.3M, the kind of oscillation that suggested frantic positioning rather than organic growth. The irony was sharp: Apostro real-time reserve verification and permissionless atomic {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} with an 82-rated backstop were still technically intact on a token trading at sixteen cents before being frozen. The {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} of the {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} margin via off-exchange settlement partners did not save the synthetic when the EOA minter was compromised. Six-chain deployment across Ethereum, Base, BSC, Berachain, HyperEVM, and Arbitrum meant the failure was visible everywhere, not just somewhere.

usdz-anzen.title: Private Credit Meets DeFi
usdz-anzen.text: Anzen's USDz is 80% backed by U.S. private credit ABS: SMB merchant receivables, factored invoices, auto leases, consumer installment lending, and litigation finance. SEC-licensed broker-dealer Percent underwrites the exposure, with 15% in Superstate tokenized {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} products and 5% cash. A mediocre peg grade and hundreds of recorded depeg events make USDz one of the more frequently depegged stablecoins on the dashboard, and its supply has contracted sharply, answering the question of what happens when holders lose confidence in private credit backing. Qualified Market Makers mint at 1:1 USDz/USDC while retail relies on DEX arbitrage to close the gap. It is a two-tier system that works when the market trusts the collateral and breaks when it doesn't. The yield from private credit is real and uncorrelated with crypto markets, but so is the liquidity mismatch between 90-day {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} receivables and instant {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} expectations against {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}-only proof.

ausd-agora.title: VanEck's Quiet Dollar
ausd-agora.text: AUSD is Agora's centralized dollar stablecoin, redeemable 1:1 and backed by cash, short-dated U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury bills{{/term}}, and overnight repos managed by VanEck. The institutional stack is unusually explicit: VanEck manages the reserves, State Street provides {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} through a bankruptcy-remote Delaware Statutory Trust, and Grant Thornton publishes monthly {{term:attestation}}reserve attestations{{/term}} rather than a token-specific real-time proof feed. Revenue sharing with distribution partners has helped its multichain rollout without changing the basic bargain: holders rely on an issuer, an asset manager, a custodian, and a periodic accountant. That is a cleaner chain than many fiat-backed dollars offer, but it is still a chain. AUSD's transparency is monthly-attestation based, not a live on-chain reserve window.

usds-sky.title: The PSM Moat Deepens
usds-sky.text: Sky Dollar still commands the single best {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} infrastructure in stablecoins: a permissionless {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} with atomic, zero-fee settlement and well over half of total supply available as immediate exit capacity. No other stablecoin at scale offers anything close. The A- safety grade reflects strength tempered by where the cracks actually are, with a reserve mix split across PSM stablecoins, Spark lending {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} positions, and Grove {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} allocations providing genuine diversification rather than the concentration risk that plagues most competitors. The peg itself is the easy part. USDS sits at the calm end of the stress scale and clears its worst sub-day wobbles within hours, with only a handful of brief deviations across the rolling window. The yield-to-risk story through the Sky Savings Rate still rewards holders without the exotic risk profiles that higher-yielding alternatives require. The structural dependency on USDC as mechanism-critical PSM collateral remains the one tension in a DAO-governed system that aspires to monetary sovereignty. Roughly a third of Sky Dollar's backing ultimately traces back to Circle's banking relationships, with {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} Maker vaults backing the rest.

m-m0.title: The Middleware Dollar
m-m0.text: Institutional dollar stablecoin minted 1:1 by permissioned issuers against short-term U.S. T-bills in bankruptcy-remote SPVs, with on-chain validator attestations replacing periodic audits; institution-facing liquidity offset by issuer redeemability. M0's M token is backed 100% by short-term {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} in bankruptcy-remote SPVs. It is a pristine reserve that earns a perfect peg score, yet the overall safety grade sits at C: the redeemability backstop and clean collateral are dragged down by centralized governance and institutional-unregulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. The tension is the familiar one: direct M liquidity stays institution-facing rather than pooled on DEXes, so Pharos leaves it unrated on liquidity, but eventual {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} gives the token a stronger exit profile than spot depth alone would suggest. Permissioned Minters lock T-bill collateral while Validators cryptographically attest sufficiency on-chain, a trust architecture that swaps auditor snapshots for protocol-level verification: elegant, but it concentrates control in a permissioned issuer set, which is exactly what holds the grade down. M's significance is downstream: it anchors the M0 infrastructure cohort that powers Noble's USDN, MetaMask's mUSD, USD.AI's USDai, Usual's USD0, and wrapped M integrations.

usdm-moneta.title: Peg in Name Only
usdm-moneta.text: Moneta's USDM is the dashboard's cleanest example of pristine reserves failing to create a usable peg. The backing is regulator-friendly: 60% {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market funds{{/term}} from Fidelity and Amundi, 40% USD bank deposits, Norwegian MiCA EMT licensing, and a Charli3 oracle {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} before each Cardano mint. The problem is brutally simple: with no meaningful observable DEX liquidity, there are no arbitrageurs to enforce the peg, so the price wanders wherever thin order books take it. The live score is still failing even if the exact number moves around, because reserve quality is not the broken part. Multi-day issuer settlement compounds the exit risk for anyone holding meaningful size. USDM is a well-backed IOU trading at whatever the market feels like, which is a stablecoin only in the most technical and least comforting sense.

satusd-river.title: The Purist's CDP
satusd-river.text: River's satUSD is a purist Omni-CDP that refuses centralized stablecoin collateral and accepts BTC, ETH, BNB, and LSTs only. That stance gives it a clean dependency story, but peg stability has paid the price through a long record of secondary-market wobble. The Omni-{{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} architecture lets users deposit collateral on one chain and mint satUSD on another through LayerZero {{term:bridge}}bridging{{/term}}, which expands distribution while importing the usual cross-chain assumptions. The {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop offers permissionless access to blue-chip collateral through {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} positions, but minimal DEX liquidity across many chains leaves the secondary market paper-thin. Decentralized governance helps the ideology column; unproven-chain sprawl and fragile liquidity keep the score from turning that ideology into comfort. satUSD is the most principled CDP in its lane, and the market keeps reminding it that principles are not bids.

usdf-astherus.title: One Exchange, One Exit
usdf-astherus.text: Aster's USDF, issued under the Astherus name before the rebrand, is a Binance-routed {{term:basis-trade}}basis-trade{{/term}} stablecoin via Ceffu MirrorX: single-CEX concentration risk where the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop, collateral, and hedge all run through one pipeline. USDF routes its entire existence through Binance. USDT collateral sits in Ceffu {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and is deployed into long-spot-plus-short-{{term:perpetual}}perpetual{{/term}} positions executed via Ceffu's MirrorX infrastructure on a single centralized exchange. The peg itself is the easy part, and the dashboard agrees: it holds an A+ peg grade and the day-to-day stress signal sits glued to the calm end of the scale, having logged only a handful of brief, modest deviations over the tracking window. The danger here is structural, not market-visible, and the report card now says so without hedging: an F overall, with the backing and economic-control pillars both flunking outright because BSC-only deployment with thin single-pool DEX liquidity means on-chain exit options are essentially decorative the moment the Binance-Ceffu pipeline that holds the collateral, runs the hedge, and gates redemptions ever hiccups. USDF is a {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} yield product wearing a stablecoin's clothes, and the single point of failure is the entire wardrobe.

usda-avalon.title: The BTC-Backed Misnomer
usda-avalon.text: Avalon USDa calls itself a BTC-backed CDP, but the reserve mix is messier: FBTC custody exposure, a large USDT leg, and assorted BTC LSTs all sit under the Bitcoin banner. The design adds 1:1 USDT convertibility, Redstone-priced collateral, HFT liquidation machinery, and LayerZero bridge distribution, which is a lot of plumbing for a token marketed as simple Bitcoin-backed dollars. Pharos keeps the collateral-quality view conservative because wrapped BTC, centralized stablecoin exposure, and permissioned mint controls are not the same thing as holding native BTC in a trustless vault. The interesting contradiction is that the liquidation machinery can look sophisticated while the holder still depends on Cobo, Fireblocks, Coinbase Prime, role-gated minting, and cross-chain infrastructure behaving well at the same time. Lately the room has been emptying: the token trades persistently soft of the dollar, thinning price coverage has driven the peg score to the floor, and with the exit and economic-control pillars both failing, the collateral book is the only pillar still above water. The overall grade is an unqualified F. Nobody published an incident report; the exits are simply visible on-chain. It is a Bitcoin stablecoin in the way a finance committee is a wallet: technically connected to the asset, heavily mediated by everyone in the room.

usdtb-ethena.title: The Load-Bearing Wall
usdtb-ethena.text: USDtb is the stable ballast in Ethena's reserve structure, designed chiefly to be held by its parent protocol rather than traded as a retail DeFi dollar. Its reserve is mostly BlackRock's BUIDL, with cash or cash-equivalent redemption reserves, issued by Anchorage Digital and held with U.S. Bank. That puts short-dated U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}} behind the token, but through a deliberately long chain of funds, custodians, issuer controls, and Ethena risk management. Direct mint-and-redeem rails and BUIDL's atomic redemption are useful exits, though they do not turn the product into a broadly liquid consumer asset. USDtb is sensible collateral for a system that wants a quiet corner of traditional finance, and a reminder that every quiet corner has several doors.

zeusd-zoth.title: The Nine-Cent Dollar
zeusd-zoth.text:
A deprecated fixed-mint RWA escrow receipt stranded around nine cents. The March 2025 exploits ended ZeUSD's life as a dollar, and nobody has published evidence of what still backs the residue.

ZeUSD's tracked V1 was never the continuing {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} it was once labeled as: the router records collateral value and debt at mint and returns exactly what was recorded on burn, with no position-health checks, no liquidation path, and deposits paused on-chain. The March 2025 exploits involved a liquidity-pool logic flaw followed by an admin-key compromise that let the attacker upgrade contracts and drain roughly $8.4M. The attack broke the platform, and the token has since traded far below peg with zero daily volume and four figures of DEX liquidity against a nominal supply in the tens of millions of units. Zoth still lists eligible {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} collateral categories, but publishes no current allocation, attestation, or proof of reserves, so the backing pillar sits at NR: a 100% known-unknown envelope that can't be scored, only distrusted. The calm stress band and zero recorded depeg events are not reassurance; a market with no volume has nothing left to stress. And the overall NR is no reprieve from the old failing grade. It means the evidence needed to grade ZeUSD at all no longer exists.

zchf-frankencoin.title: The Oracle-Free Franc
zchf-frankencoin.text:
A CHF-pegged CDP with auction-priced collateral, no oracle dependency, and no team tokens. It carries an A- card and a single-name equity position that its purist design was never meant to hold.

Frankencoin remains the most ideologically committed stablecoin on the dashboard: no foundation, no team tokens, no VC money, and no price oracles. The overall grade has climbed back to A-, with exit quality near the top of the card. The asterisk still sits in the collateral pool: a single corporate equity, BOSS (Boss Info AG), remains roughly a third of the backing. It rivals wrapped BTC as the largest position, and that single-name concentration is what keeps the backing pillar a notch below the rest of the report card. Collateral is still valued through auction-based {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} that trades capital efficiency for oracle-manipulation resistance, a tradeoff most {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} protocols wouldn't dare make, with {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} enforced through veto-governed minting limits. The peg itself is unbothered, holding near-perfect with only a handful of shallow deviations and rarely straying from the calm end of the stress scale. This is genuinely impressive for a CHF token priced against dollar reference rates on thin liquidity. On the regulatory front the pragmatism continues: the MiCA white paper that keeps ZCHF on regulated European shelves still sits in ESMA's register, and the Frankencoin Association joined the MiCA Crypto Alliance in June 2026. The thing to watch is unchanged: the gap between Frankencoin's decentralization purity and its collateral discipline.

sources.label: MiCA Crypto Alliance welcomes Frankencoin Association (26 June 2026)

usn-noon.title: Yield Portfolio, Base Token
usn-noon.text: Noon's USN is the base dollar in a yield machine that would prefer you notice the par wrapper before the credit stack. Pharos metadata shows reserves spread across private credit, CLO exposure, DeFi lending, principal tokens, and a small Treasury-bill sleeve, with Accountable providing a real-time reserve feed. Base USN does not itself accrue the yield; that job belongs to sUSN, while USN holders still rely on the same permissioned mint and redemption machinery. The setup is more transparent than many credit-backed dollars, but transparency does not ensure that private-credit liquidity arrives during stress. USN is stablecoin-shaped, yet the balance sheet underneath reads more like an institutional yield portfolio with a dollar label taped to the front.

honey-berachain.title: Proof of Liquidity's Dollar
honey-berachain.text: 1:1 basket-backed dollar on Berachain (USDC/USDT0/pyUSD/USDe) with atomic basket unwind; shallow liquidity and chain immaturity now hold the grade at C. HONEY is Berachain's native stablecoin, minted 1:1 against a basket of USDC, USDT0, pyUSD, and USDe through permissionless on-chain vaults governed by BGT holders. The redemption backstop with atomic settlement is the headline: you can always unwind HONEY into its constituent stablecoins, which is more than most basket tokens offer, and the peg itself has held tight enough to stay at the calm end of the stress scale. The C safety grade marks real progress from its D-territory days. V9 credits the basket architecture with a solid backing pillar and gives the control surface a passing mark.
