The SPV plumbing wears Saturn's logo, while the actual Saylor exposure sits one floor up in the sUSDat vault, which rotates capital into STRC, Strategy's perpetual preferred equity, through Clear Street {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and a Securitize-administered BVI fund. The split-level design is no longer a thought experiment: Bitcoin's June slide pushed Strategy to a steep discount to its own bitcoin stack. Saylor answered the gap in late July by redefining the mNAV formula rather than the balance sheet, and STRC traded roughly a quarter below par. A vault reported to be overwhelmingly concentrated in the preferred was marked around ninety cents on the dollar. Through all of it the T-bill floor under base USDat never moved. Pharos reads the peg pinned at the dollar with zero depeg events and a quietly respectable report card for the base token. The vault's advertised yield, meanwhile, leans on assumed STRC price recovery for more than half its headline number, which is a projection dressed as a coupon. USDat stays permissioned and geofenced away from the United States, the EEA, and OFAC jurisdictions, so the audience is offshore capital comfortable with KYC onboarding and an unstaking queue. It remains the cleanest expression of the thesis that crypto's next yield wave comes from being long whatever Saylor is short. June and July priced what that costs when Saylor is losing.

sources.label: Forbes: DeFi stablecoin operation built on Saylor's preferred stock on shaky ground (2026-07-28)

usdk-orki.title: Stranded on a Dead Chain
usdk-orki.text: Orki's USDK brought Liquity V2-style CDP mechanics to Swellchain, minted against WETH, weETH, rswETH, and swETH. Branch assignments are immutable, the protocol has no individual admin mint path, and collateral redemption is permissionless. This is the full Liquity ethos in miniature. The purity turned out to be the trap: Swellchain closed its bridge-withdrawal window on June 23, 2026 and ended chain operations on June 30, and an immutable protocol had no way to follow its users anywhere else. USDK never had a verified deployment outside Swellchain, so Pharos now carries it as a frozen, abandoned single-chain CDP. Any remaining positions depend on direct contract access against a network that has wound down. The design was honest minimalist plumbing whose single point of failure was the host chain itself, the one variable no amount of governance minimalism could control. Immutability meant the warning label was permanent; now so is the tombstone.

usdq-quill.title: Scroll's Liquity Outpost
usdq-quill.text: Quill's USDQ deploys Liquity V2's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} blueprint on Scroll, minting against wETH, wstETH, weETH, and notably SCR, the host chain's own token. LST collateral is familiar territory; accepting SCR ties the stablecoin's health to sentiment around the very network hosting it, a reflexivity loop that gets uncomfortable in a drawdown. Liquity-style dynamic {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} fees preserve the permissionless mechanics, while branch governance and Scroll's own maturity remain part of the control and infrastructure story. The thesis is that Scroll needs a native {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} dollar and a known architecture is the most familiar starting point. The harder question is whether the market needs another Liquity outpost badly enough to build durable exit liquidity around it.

chfau-allunity.title: The Frankfurt-Zurich Pipeline
chfau-allunity.text: CHFAU extends the Deutsche Boerse consortium's stablecoin ambitions from the euro to the Swiss franc: the same DWS-Galaxy-Flow Traders alliance behind EURAU, regulated under the same BaFin EMI license, with CHF reserves held 1:1 in segregated accounts at CRR credit institutions and statutory par {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} under MiCA Article 49. MiCA's EMT rules prohibit interest on holdings, so CHFAU competes on trust infrastructure rather than {{term:yield-bearing}}yield{{/term}}, and distribution has moved fast: launched on Ethereum in February 2026, live on Base since July via Coinbase's apps alongside Polygon and Tempo deployments, with circulation already in the tens of millions of dollars, hardly the boutique experiment its launch weeks suggested. The gap is evidentiary rather than regulatory: AllUnity's trust center still lists the independent reserve audit as coming soon, and without a dated report or a published cash-versus-HQLA split, Pharos's backing pillar grades the paperwork rather than the license. The result is a middling report card for an issuer whose entire pitch is institutional-grade infrastructure. The CHF demand thesis is real: demand spikes precisely when everything else goes wrong. A franc you cannot independently verify is only as credible as the promise behind it.

sources.label: AllUnity: CHFAU goes live on Base (July 2026)

buck-buck-assets.title: The Bitcoin Dollar Bet
buck-buck-assets.text: BUCK was Bridge Building's USDC-redeemable savings stablecoin backed by Strategy Inc. preferred stock (STRC) before its April 2026 wind-down. BUCK billed itself as "the world's first SavingsCoin": a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} stablecoin whose treasury was 77% Strategy Inc. perpetual preferred stock, making it less a dollar and more a leveraged view on MicroStrategy's Bitcoin conviction with a dollar wrapper. The yield story (targeting 7% annually via STRC dividends, distributed as monthly rebases) was compelling until you traced the dependency chain: STRC pays dividends from a company whose entire thesis is that Bitcoin goes up forever, which is either a feature or a ticking clock depending on your priors. A BVI-domiciled entity with a single-entity governance model, upgradeable proxy contracts, and a denylist controlled by ex-Uber and ex-Bird executives was not the typical stablecoin trust model, though monthly {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} from The Network Firm added a layer of professional accountability. At roughly $2 million in circulation with 261 holders and negligible DEX volume, BUCK ended its life as a micro-cap experiment in whether you can build a savings product on top of someone else's Bitcoin maximalism.

bd-basedollar.title: Liquity's Fork, Aerodrome's Yield
bd-basedollar.text: BD is now live as Base's licensed Liquity V2 fork, with {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} borrowing against ETH, wstETH, rETH, cbETH, and cbBTC rather than the Aero LP collateral its pre-launch pitch emphasized. Stability Pool depositors collect borrower and liquidation fees, while AERO and Aerodrome LP branches remain the promised second act, a sensible sequence after the audit work found and fixed a high-severity LP-price manipulation flaw. The market has started narrowly: price discovery currently rests on one BD/USDC Aerodrome stableswap pool and circulation is still modest, so a dollar print is evidence of launch, not yet evidence of depth. The control model also lands between the branding and the bytecode: existing borrowing branches are collateral-gated and the token owner is renounced, but a 2-of-6 Safe can authorize new minting branches without a token-level cap. Base Dollar has shipped the Liquity machinery; now it has to prove the Aero flywheel is more than launch copy.

wm-m0.title: M Without the Yield
wm-m0.text: wM is M0's non-rebasing ERC-20 wrapper over M, backed by short-term U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} bills in bankruptcy-remote SPVs. The price of composability is that holders volunteer to forfeit the yield. Underneath sits the same reserve framework and Validator {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} as M, while the wrapper routes accrued value to TTG-approved earner accounts through `claimExcess()`, leaving wM as a flat dollar for downstream integrations. There is no local blacklist, freeze, or pause function, and open wrap/unwrap keeps the price anchored to M through arbitrage rather than a separate reserve operation. Its multichain footprint makes wM the plumbing beneath a growing family of M0 extensions: nobody is really meant to stop at the wrapper when the yield lives one layer further down. It is the cleanest expression of M0's thesis that carry belongs to whoever puts the dollar to work, not whoever merely holds the adapter token.

usdnr-nerona.title: Private Bank, Public Plumbing
usdnr-nerona.text: Nerona's USDnr is a thin permissioned wrapper over M0's $M, a tokenized short-term {{term:treasury}}T-bill{{/term}} exposure minted through MXON, with the T-bill carry accruing to the M0 reserve and Nerona rather than holders, who are pointed at the sUSDnr staking vault if they want the yield the marketing promises. The wrapper inherits every M0-layer risk: minter insolvency, governance deactivation, and real-time Validator attestations as the only reserve telemetry. All of it sits under single-entity governance with KYC-gated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} reserved for clients of Nerona's private-wealth platform. Distribution has gone backwards: circulation peaked in the tens of millions in spring 2026 and has since collapsed by more than ninety percent to low-single-digit millions, which for a private-wealth product reads less like traction than a treasury parking spot being vacated. Mind the symbol: this is USDnr (Nerona, on Ethereum), not USDN (Noble's M0 wrapper on Cosmos). Sloppy press copy conflates the two, but they share nothing beyond the M0 plumbing underneath. A private bank for the onchain era, still waiting for depositors.

usdk-kast.title: The Anjouan Card Dollar
usdk-kast.text: KAST's USDK is an Anjouan-domiciled M0 wrapper of tokenized {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, distributed via a fintech card app. T-bill yield is retained by KAST, not passed to holders. KAST Dollar is what you get when a Comoros-domiciled fintech wraps M0's tokenized {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, slaps a card on top, and quietly pockets the yield. The token sits on Solana as a Token-2022 mint with permissioned transfer hooks and confidential-transfer extensions built in. This is useful if you trust KAST and BitGo, and awkward otherwise. At roughly $24M outstanding it is still proof-of-concept scale, riding entirely on M0 Validator {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}} rather than its own audit trail. Holders earn nothing; if you want the T-bill carry you're nudged into USDKy, KAST's separately rebasing twin. The legal stack is KAST Tech in Anjouan, {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} by partners, and a 'not a bank' disclaimer in bold. It is the modern offshore neobank uniform. A cleaner version of buying T-bills than most card-app stablecoins, provided you've made peace with single-jurisdiction issuer risk and a regulator most maps don't bother to label.

xo-exodus.title: Self-Custody's Custodial Dollar
xo-exodus.text:
MoonPay mints, M0 wraps, Exodus distributes. It is a Treasury-backed Solana token whose yield accrues to issuers and whose authorities live on a single MoonPay key.

When a self-custody wallet best known for letting users hold their own keys decides to mint its own dollar, the result is XO Cash: a MoonPay-issued, M0-wrapped {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} claim wearing an Exodus hoodie. The reserves sit in MoonPay's regulated SPVs under institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and the M0 yield quietly accrues to the issuers, not the holders, which is the polite way of saying XO is a payment rail with a stablecoin garnish. Token-2022 ships with pausable, transfer-hook, and permanent-delegate authorities all held by a single MoonPay key, so the 'self-custody' marketing applies to your wallet but not to your tokens. Initial proof of product-market fit was paying X Games athletes $2,500 signing bonuses, which is either a charming retail use case or a launch metric in search of a thesis. Backed by short-dated Treasuries, geofenced where it has to be, and aimed squarely at the Exodus Pay card audience that has never asked what an SPV is.

jpysc-sbi-startale.title: Japan trust-bank JPY stablecoin
jpysc-sbi-startale.text: JPYSC went live on June 24, 2026 as Japan's first stablecoin issued through a trust bank rather than under JPYC's prepaid-instrument workaround, and that distinction is still the entire product. Shinsei Trust & Banking issues it, SBI VC Trade distributes it, and Startale Group, the Astar Network operator and Sony's Soneium co-developer, built the rails with roughly $63M of cash-and-JGB reserves in segregated trust-account {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, under FSA-grade {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, on day one. Its Type III electronic payment instrument classification gives JPYSC the trust-law {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} rights JPYC spent three years negotiating around, asset segregation, exemption from the ¥1M transfer cap, and permission to park up to 50% of reserves in {{term:treasury}}Japanese government bonds{{/term}}, which can generate yield that the prepaid model legally cannot touch. The 'launch' remains a closed loop: only verified SBI VC Trade account holders can hold JPYSC, with no external-wallet withdrawals or public-chain circulation. Startale insists the on-chain plumbing is built and merely waiting on legal and tax clarity, not technology. Supply has grown more than fivefold since launch to north of ¥20 billion, SBI VC Trade's lending product went live in July, and a DigiFT partnership is wiring JPYSC into tokenized capital-markets settlement, all with zero secondary-market volume because there is no secondary market. That is precisely the market-gating bet: Japan's stablecoin market was gated on legal infrastructure, and SBI's institutional book plus Startale's stack is designed to capture demand when the gate opens.

rgbp-revolut.title: Revolut Pre-Launch Sterling Stablecoin
rgbp-revolut.text:
Revolut's pre-launch UK GBP stablecoin would still issue from the e-money subsidiary, not the bank, and remains sandbox-only. The Bank of England rules once called structurally unviable have been substantially softened.

Revolut got its full UK banking licence in March 2026 after a 20-month mobilisation. It then confirmed its proposed GBP stablecoin would not be issued from the new banking entity, since BoE rules constrain issuing stablecoins across affiliated subsidiaries; issuance falls back to Revolut Ltd, the e-money arm. The regulatory weather has since turned: the BoE's June 2026 final policy statement scrapped the proposed £20,000 individual holding cap in favour of a temporary per-coin issuance ceiling of roughly £40bn, and lifted the share of reserves allowed in yield-bearing short-dated UK T-bills from 60% to 70%. This change retreated from exactly the provisions legal analysts had called commercially fatal. What survives is still austere: the remaining 30% sits unremunerated at the Bank, holders receive no yield, par {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} within 24 hours is mandatory, and the timeline runs through rules finalised by end-2026, regulated sterling coins from 2027, and full UK authorisation only in October 2027. The priority use case, per Revolut's House of Lords testimony, remains the UK→India remittance corridor, the world's seventh-largest, rather than retail payments. Revolut's real asset is its millions of UK users who already open the app daily, with bank-style {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and redemption bolted on top. The BoE no longer says the product cannot work. Revolut now has to prove it should.

sources.label: BoE policy statement and draft rules on systemic stablecoins (June 2026)
CoinDesk: BoE drops holding limits, sets $50bn issuance cap
Payment Expert: Revolut UK policy head on GBP stablecoin (House of Lords)

ausdt-tether-alloy.title: Gold Collateral, Dollar Target
ausdt-tether-alloy.text: aUSDT is Alloy by Tether's dollar stablecoin: a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} where verified users deposit Tether Gold (XAUT) and mint dollars at up to 75% LTV, so the peg sits on top of {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} gold rather than a bank account. Alloy Tether turns Tether Gold into a dollar-tracking credit instrument: verified users deposit XAUT into an Ethereum vault, mint aUSDT against a 75% mint-to-value ceiling, and return aUSDT plus fees to withdraw collateral. That gives Pharos a clean on-chain reserve view because the XAUT backing sits in the CMPVault, but it also means aUSDT inherits Tether Gold {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, gold-price volatility, whitelist access, and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} mechanics. The peg rests on an overcollateralized gold position engineered to trade near one dollar, not on a bank-account promise. It is also now a position in run-off: Tether is winding down the Alloy platform, new minting is halted, and holders have until mid-September 2026 to return aUSDT and pull their XAUT collateral before the exit window closes. The experiment ends as a footnote to Tether's gold strategy: the market wanted the bullion token, not a dollar derivative of it.

usdsui-sui.title: Sui Gets Its Native Dollar
usdsui-sui.text: USDsui is Sui's native dollar issued through Bridge (Stripe), backed by short-dated {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}}/repos/MMFs. It is a native fiat-backed dollar rather than a bridged USDC. USDsui is the Sui ecosystem dollar issued through Bridge, Stripe's stablecoin infrastructure arm. The asset gives Sui a native fiat-backed stablecoin rather than another {{term:bridge}}bridged{{/term}} dollar, with DefiLlama exposing supply and price data for live peg monitoring. The reserve model is conventional Bridge Open Issuance: cash, short-dated {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}}, repos, and government {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market funds{{/term}} support mint and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}, with institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. DefiLlama supply and price data support peg monitoring, while reserve composition remains curated until Bridge publishes a USDsui-specific reserve feed or Sui supply data with stronger public verification.

brlv-crown.title: Brazilian Bonds On Chain
brlv-crown.text: BRLV is Crown's centralized Brazilian real stablecoin, mint/redeemed 1:1 for BRL and backed mostly by Brazilian federal {{term:treasury}}Treasury bonds{{/term}} in segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. Crown BRLV is a Brazilian real stablecoin backed by federal government bonds pledged for token holders through a security-agent structure. That is a cleaner reserve story than most emerging-market fiat coins: the backing is local sovereign debt rather than offshore dollar liquidity, and the legal structure is designed to keep reserve claims separate from Crown itself. The risks are equally specific: BRL liquidity, Brazilian sovereign-rate volatility, and KYC-gated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}. Pharos tracks the BRL peg directly while treating reserves as curated-validated evidence because Crown's reserve page is not yet suitable for automated reserve verification.

usdglo-glo.title: Glo Dollar Public-Goods Reserve
usdglo-glo.text: Glo Dollar is Brale-issued dollar plumbing with an unusual allocation decision: reserve yield funds public-goods causes instead of being rebated to holders, exchanges, or the issuer's distribution partners. The backing itself is deliberately ordinary, split between cash-like assets and U.S. government-backed debt with monthly attestations and 1:1 mint and redemption through Brale. That makes USDGLO's differentiation moral and distributional, not mechanical, which is more interesting than another fake innovation label. Pharos also tracks it because small stablecoins can still become meaningful dependencies when they show up inside other reserve stacks. Commercially inconvenient is currently winning: the float halved inside a month, most of it leaving Celo in a single week, and redirected yield only works when there is a float to redirect. USDGLO redirects the float rather than out-engineering Circle, which is both noble and commercially inconvenient.

usdon-ondo.title: Ondo Settlement Cash
usdon-ondo.text: USDon is the cash leg inside Ondo Global Markets, not a retail dollar trying to win every DEX pair on the internet. It is backed by U.S. dollar cash or cash equivalents in brokerage accounts and used to settle purchases and redemptions for tokenized assets under Ondo's regulated platform structure. That gives it cleaner collateral than many RWA-labeled experiments, but also whitelisted access, platform dependency, and issuer-admin controls that keep the risk model institutional. Pharos treats redemption as a Global Markets route rather than a permissionless on-chain backstop, which is the right amount of boring. USDon is settlement cash with a ticker, and pretending otherwise would only make the spreadsheet feel more exciting.

audm-macropod.title: Australia's New On-Chain Dollar
audm-macropod.text: AUDM is Macropod's institutional Australian dollar: approved clients deposit AUD into a trustee-held reserve, Macropod mints against it, and redemption runs back through the same narrow channel. This release turned up paperwork Pharos had been missing. The record now includes a quarterly Hall Chadwick agreed-upon-procedures engagement as well as the monthly self-reports, and the newest verified artefact lifted the backing pillar without moving the grade. Read the engagement before celebrating it: the procedures express no opinion, the report notes the firm was not required to be independent, and encumbrance was tested by inquiry alone, so the engagement covers arithmetic only: bank balances at Westpac and Banking Circle against on-chain supply across four networks, matching to within a rounding error, rather than any assurance that the arrangement is sound. For a float this small, quarterly no-opinion procedures are a reasonable place to start and a poor place to settle. The constraints remain scale and cadence, and the ceiling lifts when reports arrive often enough, and structured enough, for a scoring engine to actually consume them.

audf-forte.title: Australia's New Regulated Long Tail
audf-forte.text: AUDF is Forte Tech Solutions' centralized Australian dollar stablecoin, redeemable 1:1 with AUD reserves and cash-equivalent assets held in segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. Forte AUD is the straightforward version of an Australian stablecoin: issuer-run, AFSL-regulated, publicly documented, and redeemable back into bank-account AUD for eligible users. The reserve story is respectable for a long-tail fiat token because Forte publishes recurring reserve reports and legal terms instead of treating backing as a black box, but the public evidence is still PDF-based rather than a continuously queryable feed. At roughly $3.6 million in market cap, AUDF is not systemically important; the primary path back to fiat is issuer {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} for eligible users. It is interesting because the legal and reserve posture is cleaner than many niche fiat coins even while the liquidity footprint remains small.

busd0-usual.title: Fixed-Maturity USD0 Bond
busd0-usual.text: bUSD0 is Usual's bond-leg wrapper of USD0, formerly USD0++, renamed under the UIP-12 redesign: a fixed-notional bond maturing June 11, 2028 that behaves like a discount instrument, not a spot dollar, before that date. Par {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} before maturity requires pairing bUSD0 with the separately tradeable rt-bUSD0 early-exit right, while standalone bUSD0 can trade below one dollar; yield arrives as daily USUAL token coupons rather than dollar NAV growth, so holders stack USD0 reserve quality, Usual DAO parameter risk, and pre-maturity discount risk. The product keeps evolving around its holders: the Usual Stability Loan that lets bUSD0 collateralize USD0 borrowing migrated from Euler to Fira in January 2026, and the underlying USD0 claim remains an {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} stack. Pharos has held the listing in quarantine since mid-July 2026 because none of its permitted market-data sources report a positive circulating supply or market cap: a fitting limbo for a bond that renamed itself out of the stablecoin category, only for the data feeds to agree it is not quite a dollar.

susde-ethena.title: Ethena's Savings Sleeve
susde-ethena.text: sUSDe is the yield wrapper over USDe, converting Ethena staking rewards into a rising exchange rate rather than a separate payout. Economically it inherits the same USDe reserve and custody stack: liquid stablecoin backing, delta-neutral BTC and ETH/LST hedges, off-exchange custody, CEX execution, and the operational choreography that keeps the synthetic dollar flat. The wrapper's separate risk is exit timing, because unstaking burns the receipt immediately while the holder still waits through Ethena's cooldown flow before receiving liquid USDe. Pharos therefore treats sUSDe as a wrapper dependency, not a diversified asset that magically escapes the parent risk. It is USDe with yield accounting and a waiting room, which is useful as long as nobody confuses the waiting room for a fire exit.

susds-sky.title: The Plain Sky Savings Token
susds-sky.text: sUSDS is the plain savings receipt in the Sky stack: deposit USDS, receive an ERC-4626-style token whose exchange rate compounds with the Sky Savings Rate. That simplicity is the point, especially next to stUSDS, which pushes holders into risk-capital exposure and borrower shortfall risk. The wrapper still inherits the USDS reserve mix, Sky governance, and the USDS PSM exit surface, so it is not detached from the parent system just because the vault interface is clean. Pharos reads sUSDS as the clean yield-bearing expression of Sky's base dollar, not a separate reserve design. Sometimes the least theatrical wrapper is the one doing the least damage, which in stablecoins is a compliment.

sdai-sky.title: The Classic DSR Wrapper
sdai-sky.text:
The original Dai savings receipt: deposit DAI and accrue the DSR through a rising exchange rate, with wrapper-contract risk on top of DAI-tier CDP risk.

sDAI is the original Dai savings receipt: deposit DAI, receive a token whose redeemable DAI balance grows with the Dai Savings Rate. It adds very little conceptual complexity beyond the base asset, but it still belongs on its own row because holders are choosing a NAV-appreciating {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper with its own liquidity, integrations, and wrapper-contract risk rather than plain DAI. The underlying still inherits DAI's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} collateral profile.

sfrxusd-frax.title: Frax's Yield Sleeve
sfrxusd-frax.text: sfrxUSD is the savings sleeve for frxUSD, not a second Frax dollar with its own reserve book. Depositors trade the flat base token for a vault share whose exchange rate rises as Frax routes frxUSD income and custodian yield into the wrapper. That distinction matters: wrapper risk is share accounting, redemption mechanics, and liquidity for sfrxUSD, while the parent stablecoin risk remains the frxUSD custodian and reserve stack. The multichain footprint makes the token easier to hold, but it also turns a simple Treasury-style reserve story into Frax governance, issuer controls, and bridge-aware exit math wearing a tidy yield label.

scrvusd-curve.title: Borrower Interest Receipt
scrvusd-curve.text: scrvUSD is Curve's ERC-4626 savings share over crvUSD, so the wrapper adds yield and exchange-rate behavior without inventing a new dollar. Deposited crvUSD backs the share, while borrower interest and protocol revenue make the redeemable crvUSD balance climb over time. The wrapper risk is vault accounting, liquidity, and the ability to exit back into crvUSD; the parent risk is still Curve's CDP and LLAMMA machinery, with BTC and ETH collateral doing the heavy lifting underneath. It is the polite version of leverage plumbing: cleaner to hold than raw crvUSD, but absolutely not detached from the machinery that mints the base asset.

cusdo-openeden.title: Non-Rebasing OpenDollar
cusdo-openeden.text: cUSDO is OpenEden's non-rebasing wrapper for USDO, built for protocols that would rather watch a price rise than reconcile changing balances. It keeps the same underlying OpenDollar claim: tokenized {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} exposure and issuer-controlled {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} rails, but moves the yield expression into NAV appreciation. That makes the product mechanically useful without making the reserve chain any shorter: cUSDO still depends on USDO, OpenEden, and the underlying tokenized T-bill stack. Its move from F to D this release is borrowed rather than earned: nothing about the wrapper itself was re-examined; a child simply cannot rate above its required parent, and USDO's evidence upgrade raised the ceiling cUSDO has been sitting under. The wrapper's own admin surface is a single key holding upgrade and pause authority across three EVM deployments, so composability does not equal neutrality. cUSDO is a formatting layer over the same dollar claim, and in DeFi, formatting layers have a habit of becoming risk layers.

syusd-aegis.title: Aegis Cooldown Wrapper
syusd-aegis.text: sYUSD is Aegis's staking wrapper over YUSD, capitalizing funding-rate income into a rising exchange rate instead of paying out a separate coupon. The parent stablecoin risk is YUSD's BTC spot plus short-perpetual hedge model and off-exchange custody assumptions; the wrapper risk is the ERC-4626 vault, bridge footprint, and seven-day cooldown before holders get back to liquid YUSD. Accountable provides real-time reserve visibility, which is useful, but it does not turn a delta-neutral basis trade into a bank deposit. The product is different enough from YUSD to deserve its own row and similar enough that anyone pretending the risks are independent is doing spreadsheet theater.

stusds-sky.title: Sky Risk-Capital USDS
stusds-sky.text: Sky's expert-mode risk-capital module over USDS that funds SKY-backed borrowing and absorbs shortfall via slashing. stUSDS is Sky's expert-mode risk-capital token, not a plain sUSDS savings receipt. Deposited USDS funds SKY-backed borrowing while idle liquidity earns the Sky Savings Rate, exposing holders to borrower shortfall, governance slashing, utilization, and withdrawal-liquidity risk. As a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} module distinct from passive {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} paths, it inherits the broad Sky/USDS ecosystem and ranks differently from USDS and sUSDS because its value can be affected by staked-SKY loan performance.

stcusd-cap.title: Cap Yield Wrapper
stcusd-cap.text:
Cap's ERC-4626 staked wrapper of cUSD where operators borrow reserves against restaker collateral and repay above hurdle rate. It adds operator, restaker, and vault risk on top.

stcUSD is the {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} version of Cap cUSD. Users stake cUSD into an ERC-4626 vault while Cap operators borrow reserve assets against restaker collateral and repay with yield above the hurdle rate. Cap's design attempts to keep stablecoin holders whole through {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and slashing, but stcUSD still adds operator, restaker, strategy, and vault risk on top of the underlying cUSD basket and its {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanics.

said-gaib.title: AI Infrastructure NAV Token
said-gaib.text:
GAIB's staked AID vault token floats with the NAV of AI infrastructure financing positions. It has a different asset profile from AID's stable base.

sAID is GAIB's staked AID vault token. Unlike AID, which is intended as the stable base currency backed by {{term:treasury}}Treasuries{{/term}} and accepted stablecoins, sAID floats with the NAV of AI infrastructure financing positions plus stable reserve buffers, a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper sitting on a private credit book. Monthly withdrawal cycles, unrealized-loss-aware unstaking NAV, and private AI financing exposure make it a materially different asset from AID.

msy-main-street.title: Death by Parent
msy-main-street.text: msY was Main Street's ERC-4626-style {{term:yield-bearing}}yield share{{/term}} over msUSD, accruing value from the protocol's options and derivatives strategy while final exit ran back through msUSD's capacity-managed USDC {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}. That layering stopped being theoretical on June 20, 2026: reserve verifier Accountable terminated its contract over inadequate proof of reserves, msUSD collapsed to cents on the dollar, and the vault share, with no independent backing of its own, followed the parent down. The unwind also jammed the side exits, with the Morpho msY/USDC lending market pinned at full utilization while roughly $18 million sat trapped inside. Pharos now carries msY as frozen, a derivative casualty of counterparty failure rather than an active dollar instrument. The original risk disclosure covered strategy, {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, and liquidity risk stacked on top of base redemption. That turned out to be the whole story, except the base redemption never showed up.

yusd-yieldfi.title: YieldFi USDC Strategy Vault
yusd-yieldfi.text: YieldFi's yUSD is an ERC-4626 share over USDC that its manager routes into Pendle principal tokens, Morpho and Silo vaults, private credit, and hedged carry. The manager makes discretionary allocations while the product wears a dollar's clothing. Its backing pillar scores near the top of the scale, and that is reliably the least informative figure on the card: what backs yUSD on paper is USDC, while what determines whether it holds a dollar is allocator judgement and the exit terms of venues under no obligation to be liquid on your schedule. Nothing moved this release, which changes the reading not at all, because the D was never coming from the reserve. Economic control sits at the floor for a concrete reason: alongside deposit-minted shares, the manager holds a discretionary mint-and-burn path with no supply ceiling, gated on roles that two externally owned accounts can grant or revoke instantly. Add an exit pillar with no comparable same-notional route out, and the grade is doing precisely what it should. Pharos tracks this apart from Aegis YUSD and YO Protocol's yoUSD because the name collision conceals a different issuer and a very different risk.

sbold-k3-capital.title: K3 Stability Pool BOLD
sbold-k3-capital.text:
A K3-managed ERC-4626 wrapper around BOLD deployed into Liquity V2 Stability Pools. It earns interest and liquidation gains while adding vault, oracle, and solver risk.

sBOLD is K3 Capital's ERC-4626 wrapper around BOLD deposited into Liquity V2 Stability Pools. It earns interest and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} gains while automating the conversion of liquidated ETH and LST collateral back into BOLD. The base BOLD system is immutable and fully on-chain with {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-based issuance, but sBOLD adds K3-controlled vault, oracle, solver, and fee-switch risk, so it belongs as a separate wrapper exposure.

ybold-yearn.title: Yearn's BOLD Stability Pool Vault
ybold-yearn.text:
Yearn's ERC-4626 wrapper deploys BOLD into Liquity V2 Stability Pools, layering vault and strategy risk onto Liquity's CDP-redemption design.

yBOLD is Yearn's ERC-4626 wrapper around BOLD deposited into Liquity V2 Stability Pool strategies. It is a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper that auto-compounds {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} rewards from Liquity's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} system. It keeps the economic exposure anchored to BOLD while automating allocation across Stability Pools and liquidation-reward compounding through Yearn-managed strategy contracts. Holders can {{term:redemption}}redeem{{/term}} the vault share back into BOLD at the live exchange rate, but the exposure is not the same as holding base BOLD: it adds Yearn vault governance, strategy execution, auction, and smart-contract risk on top of Liquity's collateral-redemption design.

stkgho-umbrella-aave.title: Aave Umbrella GHO Staking
stkgho-umbrella-aave.text: Aave Umbrella stkGHO is a slashable staking receipt over GHO, which made it much more interesting than a passive savings wrapper and much less comfortable to hold during a deficit event. Depositors earn Umbrella rewards, but they also accept cooldowns, withdrawal windows, and automated loss absorption if covered GHO shortfalls materialize. Durable GHO issuance still inherits Aave's facilitator and governance controls underneath. Pharos therefore treats stkGHO as a risk-absorption asset, not a cleaner version of the base CDP stablecoin, with the non-slashable sGHO vault as the designated savings lane for anyone who never wanted the insurance job. That job is now being retired: a late-June governance vote approved sunsetting the GHO Umbrella market. Emissions and target liquidity wound to zero, the deficit offset padded so existing stakers can exit in order, and future GHO shortfalls handed to the DAO treasury instead. The yield here was payment for being useful when something goes wrong, and Aave has concluded it no longer needs to outsource that usefulness. That leaves stkGHO as a receipt for a risk the protocol is taking back in-house.

sources.label: Aave governance: Umbrella Parameter Update ARFC (GHO Umbrella sunset)
Aave Umbrella documentation (sGHO and Umbrella staking)

myrc-blox.title: Assurance Found, Composition Expired
myrc-blox.text: MYRC is Malaysia's first ringgit stablecoin, issued by Blox and gated through MyKad eKYC to Malaysian residents with a linked local bank account, a deliberately small, deliberately domestic product with a float in the low millions of ringgit. This release moves it in two opposite directions at once. A verification pass found what an earlier one had missed: Tommy Ung & Partners PLT really are issuing monthly ISAE 3000 reasonable-assurance opinions that MYR assets held equal or exceed MYRC in circulation, a recurring third-party reconciliation of the strongest kind short of a full audit, which lifts economic control off the floor and the card from D to C+. But the same June examination re-anchored the composition date, pushing the reserve split, mostly ringgit bank cash with the remainder in a Shariah-compliant {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}}, outside the 31-day freshness window, so backing is now scored against no admitted composition at all and a missing-composition ceiling binds the card. The irony is exact: the report that proved the reserves are real is too old to describe them. Blox still holds no Bank Negara or Securities Commission licence and its own term sheet concedes MYRC is not electronic money, so the auditor is doing all of the supervisory work here.

krwq-iq.title: First Korean Won stablecoin, RWA-backed
krwq-iq.text: First 1:1 KRW stablecoin from IQ/Frax, transitioning from USDC backing to a Korean T-bond-heavy reserve via Etherfuse Stablebonds; KYC-gated institutional access. KRWQ is the first stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the South Korean won, launched October 2025 by IQ in partnership with Frax. It uses LayerZero's Omnichain Fungible Token (OFT) standard with Ethereum as the canonical mint chain and Base as the primary bridged destination, sharing unified supply across deployments. Reserves are transitioning from initial USDC backing toward a target mix dominated by short-term Korean Treasury Bonds, which are tokenized through Etherfuse's Stablebond framework and held in segregated, bankruptcy-remote custody at Shinhan Securities, alongside USDC and Frax frxUSD. Mint and redemption are KYC-gated to institutional counterparties (exchanges, market makers, OTC desks), and KRWQ is explicitly not marketed to South Korean residents while domestic stablecoin legislation moves through the National Assembly. The transparency stack took a real step in June when KRWQ became the first Korean won stablecoin wired into Chainlink Proof of Reserve for automated verification, though the promised independent monthly attestations still lack a named auditor. Reserves anchor on tokenized Korean {{term:treasury}}treasury bonds{{/term}} as {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} held in segregated Shinhan Securities {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, with KYC-gated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and LayerZero OFT acting as the cross-chain {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}}.

reur-royal-euro.title: Delisted Into the Dark
reur-royal-euro.text:
A delisted euro token from RIB Digital Holdings whose public markets vanished and whose self-reported reserve snapshots stalled months earlier.

Pharos no longer tracks REUR as an active stablecoin: AscendEX delisted its only identified public markets at the end of June 2026, and the issuer now describes access through approved institutional, OTC, and private settlement channels. There is no ordinary public route to acquire or redeem this euro. Transparency decayed in parallel: the self-signed proof-of-reserves snapshots, pitched as near-real-time, stalled in late April 2026 and have not been updated since. What remains is a Hong Kong-domiciled euro claim on issuer-managed bank deposits, with self-reported reserves and discretionary {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} terms doing all the load-bearing work. A stablecoin you cannot publicly buy, verify, or exit is a private IOU wearing a ticker.

sources.label: AscendEX RUSD and REUR delisting notice
RIB Digital transparency page (snapshot series stalled April 2026)

kgst-kyrgyz-som.title: Central Asia's On-Chain Som
kgst-kyrgyz-som.text: Kyrgyz som stablecoin on BNB Chain claiming 1:1 KGS bank reserves; no verified attestation cadence, USD normalization via secondary FX feeds. KGST is a Kyrgyz som stablecoin tracked by CoinGecko on BNB Chain. It is presented as a fully backed 1:1 KGS token, giving Pharos a direct Central Asian local-currency peg, but public reserve and redemption materials remain limited compared with established regulated fiat issuers. KGST also depends on secondary FX feeds for USD normalization because CoinGecko does not currently expose a native KGS quote. Without a verified cadence of {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, transparent {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, or a documented {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} window, the issuer's 1:1 claim remains unaudited by Pharos.

audx-aussie-dollar-token.title: AUD Liquidity With Sparse Footing
audx-aussie-dollar-token.text: AUDX is TAU Pty Ltd's centralized Australian dollar stablecoin, designed for 1:1 AUD {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and backed by AUD cash and government-backed instruments. AUDX is an Australian dollar stablecoin issued by Tau Pty Ltd, trading as AUDX Token, and tracked by CoinGecko across Ethereum, Polygon, and Conflux. The issuer describes AUSTRAC registration and 1:1 AUD reserves held in regulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} at financial institutions. Market depth is still small, so Pharos treats the reserve story as useful but less battle-tested than older AUD rails with longer public operating histories.

cngn-compliant-naira.title: Naira Settlement Goes Multichain
cngn-compliant-naira.text: cNGN is a Nigerian naira stablecoin that looks more like regulated settlement infrastructure than a speculative dollar substitute. The reserve mix is split between commercial-bank naira deposits and naira money-market or short-term FGN treasury-bill exposure, with monthly independent attestations noted in Pharos metadata. Nigerian SEC oversight gives it a clearer regulatory anchor than most local-currency experiments, though that does not magically create deep secondary liquidity. The multichain footprint improves utility for payments and exchange settlement, while issuer-controlled Safes and a Solana mint key keep governance firmly centralized. The argument is starting to attract builders. HyperFX, a new on-chain FX engine, settles its naira leg in cNGN. cNGN's best argument is the utility of compliant naira rails, precisely because everyone else keeps trying to dollarize the problem.

brl1-brl1.title: Small-Cap Real Exposure
brl1-brl1.text: BRL1 is a centralized Brazilian real stablecoin, targeting a 1:1 peg with a BRL reserve mix of Brazilian {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} ETFs, repo agreements, and cash equivalents. BRL1 is a Brazilian real stablecoin tracked by CoinGecko on Polygon. It adds another BRL-denominated route alongside the older Brazilian real tokens in Pharos, but with a smaller operating footprint and less public reserve transparency than the most established local issuers, including the absence of regular third-party {{term:attestation}}attestations{{/term}}. Pharos therefore models the peg as issuer-backed while keeping disclosure confidence conservative.

wars-argentine-peso.title: ARS Peg With Split Signals
wars-argentine-peso.text: WARS is an Argentine peso stablecoin from Ripio's wFIAT suite, tracked across six EVM chains with the same contract address but weaker reserve and redemption confidence than major fiat issuers. WARS is an Argentine peso stablecoin tracked by DefiLlama across Ethereum, Base, World Chain, BNB Chain, Polygon, and Gnosis, with CoinGecko also listing the token below the current $1M market-cap threshold. That split makes it eligible through DefiLlama coverage but still a higher-uncertainty addition: the same contract address appears across the EVM deployments via {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} infrastructure, while ARS {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} confidence remain weaker than major fiat issuers.

pusd-polymarket.title: The Prediction-Market Wrapper
pusd-polymarket.text:
An application-tier dollar balance token mapped to USDC on Polygon, with risk concentrated in the Polymarket app rails rather than a new reserve.

Polymarket USD is the dollar balance token used around Polymarket deposits and withdrawals on Polygon. Its collateral story is simple: the token is intended to map to USDC and USDC.e in Polymarket rails, so reserve risk is mostly wrapper, {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}}, and app-access risk rather than a new asset mix. Pharos enables curated reserve validation against the Polygon contract and keeps the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path documented through Polymarket docs. Scale is the new fact: supply has swelled into the hundreds of millions on prediction-market volume. An election cycle and a World Cup will do that, which makes the wrapper's app-rail risk a materially bigger number than it was in spring, even as the peg record stays spotless. The token functions as an application dollar, not an independent issuer reserve.

rusd-royal-dollar.title: Private Settlement Only
rusd-royal-dollar.text:
A delisted Royal/R Coins dollar whose reserve questions were never answered before its public markets disappeared.

Royal Dollar is no longer tracked as an active stablecoin: AscendEX delisted the only identified public RUSD markets at the end of June 2026, and the issuer now describes access through approved institutional, OTC, and private settlement channels. No ordinary public acquisition or redemption route remains. The transparency questions that dogged the token while listed were never resolved on the way out: reserve composition and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanics stayed too opaque to model as a high-quality fiat backstop, and Pharos's reserve validation was limited to confirming tracked on-chain supply against a curated view. The Hong Kong-domiciled issuer's discretionary redemption terms and KYC-gated processes now operate entirely out of public sight, alongside sister token REUR, which exited through the same door on the same day. A dollar claim that leaves the public market before publishing a real {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} is not a stablecoin story that gets a second act.

sources.label: AscendEX RUSD and REUR delisting notice

usdr-ring.title: The Ring Protocol Dollar
usdr-ring.text: Ring Protocol's USDR is a small crypto-backed synthetic dollar with modest documentation; the dashboard models the reserve stack conservatively as protocol collateral and liquidity positions. Ring USD is a crypto-backed synthetic dollar from Ring Protocol. Its public footprint is small, so the dashboard models the reserve stack conservatively as protocol collateral and liquidity positions rather than a granular attested basket. The Ethereum supply is eligible for curated reserve validation, but {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} quality still depends on Ring-specific mechanics and protocol liquidity. That makes USDR a long-tail collateralized dollar with meaningful smart-contract and governance dependency.

uusd-anything-labs.title: The BSC Unity Dollar
uusd-anything-labs.text: Unity USD is a small BSC dollar token from Anything Labs with limited public reserve detail. Pharos tracks it with a high-risk reserve slice and conservative redemption assumptions. Unity USD is a BSC dollar token from the UUSD/Anything Labs ecosystem. The collateral and peg design are presented as protocol managed via {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} mechanics, but public reserve detail is limited, so Pharos uses a single high-risk reserve slice rather than implying precision. The BSC contract is tracked for supply and curated reserve validation. Until clearer reserve proofs are available, UUSD remains a small, governance-dependent crypto-backed stablecoin where {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} parameters and exit liquidity are not externally verifiable.

jusd-jusd-stable-token.title: The Small Multichain Dollar
jusd-jusd-stable-token.text: Long-tail multichain USD token (BSC + Polygon) with issuer/protocol-managed crypto collateral; reserve composition unverified. JUSD is a long-tail dollar token with BSC and Polygon contracts and issuer/protocol documentation. Pharos models its reserves as protocol-managed crypto collateral because public materials do not provide a reviewed, granular collateral breakdown. The BSC deployment is used for curated validation, while Polygon is kept for discovery. Its main risk is not the stated dollar target, but the limited transparency around reserve composition and live redemption depth. Until JUSD publishes a third-party {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} and discloses {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop and reserve quality remain unmodelled by Pharos.

jusd-juicedollar.title: Bitcoin-backed dollar on Citrea
jusd-juicedollar.text: Citrea-native BTC-collateralized USD using a Frankencoin/d-EURO oracle-free CDP architecture; sub-$1M cap, early-network depth is the main risk. Juice Dollar is a Citrea-native USD stablecoin minted from BTC collateral in overcollateralized positions. The design follows the Frankencoin / d-EURO lineage: no external price oracle, no admin-key intervention path in the published docs, on-chain collateral positions, and liquidation mechanics instead of issuer custody. CoinGecko classifies JUSD as a Citrea ecosystem crypto-backed stablecoin, but current public market cap is still sub-$1M, so the main risk is early-network depth and liquidation-market maturity rather than off-chain reserve opacity. The model is a Frankencoin-style {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} with on-chain {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and bidding-based {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} standing in for an external oracle.

usda-alpha-partner.title: The Alpha Partner Dollar
usda-alpha-partner.text: Alpha Partner USDA is a BSC-only dollar token with more ambition than disclosure, which is a familiar ratio in the long tail. The issuer describes protocol-managed collateral and liquidity reserves, but the metadata still has no credible reserve composition, no independent attestation, and no documented mint or redemption mechanics beyond a role-gated token contract. Pharos can validate the tracked on-chain supply and record the blacklistable, admin-heavy control surface; it cannot turn vague collateral language into a clean backstop. The FDIC-style marketing claims are especially unhelpful because stablecoin reserves do not become insured just by borrowing bank vocabulary. USDA belongs in coverage, but the confidence level should stay low until the issuer publishes something less ornamental.

xdai-gnosis.title: The Native Gnosis Dollar
xdai-gnosis.text:
Gnosis Chain's native gas token is an economic claim on bridged DAI, so its peg quality cascades from Maker/Sky and Gnosis bridge infrastructure.

xDAI is the native gas token of Gnosis Chain and is economically tied to DAI {{term:bridge}}bridged{{/term}} into the network. Unlike a normal ERC-20 stablecoin, its canonical supply is native-chain accounting, so Pharos lists the WXDAI wrapper as a traded contract rather than using it as the supply contract. The reserve view is a DAI {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} dependency, making peg quality depend on Maker/Sky DAI, itself a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-backed dollar, and Gnosis bridge infrastructure. It is more infrastructure dollar than issuer token.

usdx-kava.title: The Legacy Kava Debt Dollar
usdx-kava.text: Kava USDX is a legacy {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} debt token trading well below peg, kept in the catalog as a historical depeg case rather than a healthy par dollar. Kava USDX is the older Kava Mint {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} debt token backed by crypto collateral and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} mechanics, sustained by {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} that has not been enough to defend the peg in practice. The asset remains visible in DefiLlama provider data, but its market price has spent extended periods below the dollar target, so Pharos flags it as a legacy depeg-risk entry. There is no supported canonical token contract to attach for reserve sync. Its tracking value is mostly historical and analytical: it shows how a live provider entry can coexist with a prior depeg narrative.

xtusd-xt.title: XT.com XSC CDP Dollar
xtusd-xt.text: XTUSD is XT.com's exchange-issued dollar, and its live deployment on XSC is a Maker-style Vat carrying one debt-bearing collateral type: roughly 4.3 million XTUSD borrowed against Wrapped XT. What the on-chain read found is what is missing. No Spotter, price feed, or other update contract is authorized on that Vat. The collateral price sits at a fixed value with no identified mechanism to move it. No Cat, Dog, auction, or global-settlement module is authorized either. The 2022 announcement that promised a 150% minimum collateral ratio and an auction for risky vaults is half true: the 3% annual fee matches the Jug's duty exactly, so the interest accrues as advertised, while the auction it is supposed to protect has no contract standing behind it. The Median/OSM/Spotter stack that does exist on XSC is wired to the issuer's legacy TAI deployment, not to this one. Pharos rates XTUSD NR rather than badly: an unpriced, unliquidatable vault lacks the machinery a grade would measure.

hbd-hive.title: The Hive Conversion Dollar
hbd-hive.text: HBD is Hive's {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} dollar redeemable on-chain for $1 of HIVE via witness-set conversion, with haircut rules when system debt exceeds thresholds. Hive Backed Dollar is a protocol-native dollar claim inside the Hive ecosystem. It targets $1 through HIVE conversion rules and witness-set savings parameters, not through cash or Treasury {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. That makes the collateral base reflexive to the value and governance of Hive itself, especially under haircut conditions. Pharos classifies HBD as crypto-backed and decentralized while flagging that the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop is protocol conversion capacity, not liquid off-chain reserves. That distinction the market priced in earnest in late July 2026, when HBD slid roughly a tenth below the dollar on sparse venues before clawing back to within a few percent of the peg. The defense mechanism is conversion into the very asset holders are fleeing, which is why the stress gauge sits at watch even as the quote drifts home.

jpyc-jpyc-v1.title: The Legacy JPYC Series
jpyc-jpyc-v1.text: Legacy prepaid-payment yen token series predating JPYC's funds-transfer-token migration; retained only for discovery and validation. JPY Coin v1 is the older JPYC token series, separate from the current JPYC deployment already tracked by Pharos. It is backed by yen-denominated reserve obligations and legacy redemption processes rather than the newer funds-transfer-token contracts. The Ethereum, Polygon, and Gnosis deployments are retained for discovery and reserve validation. Its main reason to track separately is migration clarity, because the old and current JPYC contracts are not interchangeable. The legacy prepaid {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} model and its narrower {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} processes are the reason v1 is not interchangeable with the current FSA-licensed JPYC contract.

nxusd-nereus.title: The Nereus CDP Dollar
nxusd-nereus.text: Small Avalanche CDP stablecoin minted by Nereus Finance against overcollateralized lending positions; now largely dormant, with a near-peg price that reflects an absence of trading rather than a working redemption arbitrage. NXUSD is a crypto-backed debt token minted through Nereus Finance on Avalanche via {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} mechanics, and its market has gone quiet: daily volume is measured in single-digit dollars, and the price drifts just below par because almost nobody trades it at all. The pristine peg score is earned the cheap way: a token that barely changes hands cannot deviate, which is why Pharos pairs it with failing exit and economic-control grades rather than taking the calm at face value. The reserve stack is modeled as {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} lending positions, which leaves the notional backing dependent on collateral volatility, {{term:liquidation}}liquidations{{/term}}, and protocol governance, none of it verified by a liquid par {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path. NXUSD fits the dormant CDP relic pattern: transparent enough to track, illiquid enough that the tracking mostly documents stillness.

wemix-dollar-wemix.title: The WEMIX Ecosystem Dollar
wemix-dollar-wemix.text: WEMIX Dollar has completed the arc its replacement plan wrote for it: the Foundation moved the ecosystem's dollar activity to bridged USDC.e, withdrew its liquidity from WEMIX$ pools, and ended swap support across WEMIX.Fi and WEMIX PLAY in April 2026, and Pharos formally froze the listing on 2026-07-11 as a confirmed wind-down. What remains is an orderly wind-down rather than a collapse. Holders kept a conversion route through the WEMIX$ Module and a longer claim window for discontinued pools, which is more exit courtesy than most retired stablecoins ever extend. The design was always an issuer-managed ecosystem unit. It had USDC backing in the WEMIX3.0 Treasury with DIOS stabilization on a chain Pharos never indexed, so outside validation of the reserves was never possible, and now it never will be. Its epitaph doubles as the genre's lesson: a game-chain dollar that never escaped its home chain proved easier to replace with another issuer's dollar than to keep running.

suiusde-sui.title: Sui Ethena-Style Synthetic Dollar
suiusde-sui.text: suiUSDe is Sui's Ethena-whitelabel synthetic dollar. The token keeps USDe's design while adding a new chain label. The reserve logic inherits Ethena-style digital-asset collateral, delta-neutral hedging, basis-trade execution, off-exchange custody, and the operational dependency on exchanges and custodians that make the parent design work. The Sui-specific twist is deployment control: a single admin role holder also controls the package upgrade path, so chain-native does not mean governance-light. Pharos tracks the Sui contract and DefiLlama visibility while keeping reserve confidence conservative because live Sui reserve checks remain unintegrated. The asset is a synthetic-dollar export, and exports tend to carry the paperwork of the country they came from.

vcred-vcred.title: The Hemi Credit Dollar
vcred-vcred.text: vCRED is a Hemi-based credit stable asset with thin public reserve detail. Pharos classifies the backing as protocol credit and crypto collateral, with no verified fiat reserve. vCRED is a Hemi-based credit stable asset with limited public reserve granularity. Pharos adds the Hemi contract and treats the backing as protocol credit and crypto collateral via {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} rather than a verified fiat reserve. The curated reserve sync can validate supply on the configured EVM chain, but it cannot validate the off-chain or strategy quality behind the collateral. The result is a tracked but high-risk long-tail dollar where {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} parameters and redemption depth remain operationally opaque.

mai-qidao.title: Debt That Cannot Be Liquidated
mai-qidao.text: MAI is a multi-collateral {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} dollar whose most important number is not its supply but the share of its loan book that no longer functions. An on-chain sweep of 71 QiDao vault contracts across twelve chains found roughly 2.1 million MAI of recorded vault debt, and about 72% of it sits in fifteen Fantom markets where every price source reverts. Because the price call fails, {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}}, collateral withdrawal, and new borrowing all revert with it: this is Multichain-era debt that cannot be cleared, only waited out, and QiDao's own site describes the Fantom position as a dispute whose tokens return to holders once resolved. The markets that do still price read exactly one Chainlink feed with no staleness check, no heartbeat enforcement, and no fallback, and no deployment carries a stability pool or insurance fund. The stabilityPool address is zero everywhere it was probed. Even on live chains some vaults are too far underwater to liquidate at all, because the collateral payout underflows before the keeper can be paid. The F grade is not a verdict on QiDao's design so much as an accounting of what is left standing.

spusd-soulpeg.title: The SoulPeg Dollar
spusd-soulpeg.text:
A small BSC dollar wrapping a soul-bound sUSDC position via Venus lending; no Pharos-reviewed holder USDC exit path makes it protocol-dependent.

SoulPeg USD is a BSC dollar token with protocol-managed collateral and liquidity. Public docs support the basic peg and contract metadata but do not expose enough reserve detail for a granular basket, so Pharos therefore uses a high-risk curated reserve slice and validates the BSC supply path. Until {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and reserve data become more transparent, spUSD remains a small protocol-dependent dollar rather than a high-confidence stablecoin.

inalpha-nest.title: The Nest Vault Share
inalpha-nest.text: NAV-priced dollar vault token holding private/structured credit with nTBILL and stablecoin buffers; not a par stablecoin. Nest Alpha Vault LP is included because providers classify it as a dollar-referenced asset, but its behavior is closer to a NAV share than a par stablecoin. The token can appreciate or drift with vault strategy performance, so Pharos marks it yield-bearing and NAV-style. Reserve validation checks the on-chain token, while the reserve slice remains the Nest Alpha strategy book. This is useful coverage, but direct comparisons with cash-backed dollars are misleading. The underlying mix is {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} credit with an nTBILL {{term:treasury}}T-bill{{/term}} buffer, so {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} depth depends on the vault's liquid stablecoin layer rather than direct par exit.

eusd-telcoin.title: The Telcoin Bank Dollar
eusd-telcoin.text: Telcoin eUSD is a bank-issued dollar token from Telcoin Digital Asset Bank, operating under Nebraska's digital-asset depository framework rather than the usual offshore issuer maze. That regulatory posture is stronger than most long-tail additions, but Pharos still keeps the reserve slice conservative because detailed public telemetry and published monthly attestations are not yet as mature as the charter story. The token spans Ethereum, Base, Polygon, and Solana, with issuer and multisig controls doing the minting work behind the scenes. Redemption is a KYC-gated banking-rail process, not a permissionless DeFi backstop, so the trust boundary is the bank. The charter started paying rent in June, when Telcoin launched the first U.S. regulated on-chain bank accounts tied natively to eUSD through its Wallet V5: deposit banking and a stablecoin sharing one regulated container. eUSD is what happens when a stablecoin gets a bank charter before it gets market depth, and the bank part is no longer theoretical.

money-defi-money.title: The defi.money Stablecoin
money-defi-money.text: MONEY is defi.money's crypto-backed loan stablecoin, closer to a crvUSD-style CDP than to a fixed reserve wrapper with tidy bank statements. Users deposit approved collateral such as WBTC and ETH, borrow against market-specific risk parameters, and rely on conversion ranges and liquidations to keep the system solvent. Pharos treats the reserve as protocol-approved crypto loan collateral and validates it through curated on-chain checks, but the live collateral mix is still less transparent than the larger CDP systems it echoes. The mint path is user-collateralized, while market onboarding and debt ceilings remain under partially bounded admin control. It is a serious fork of a serious design, which still leaves plenty of room for governance knobs to matter.

fusd-freedom-dollar.title: The Zano Privacy Dollar
fusd-freedom-dollar.text: FUSD is a Zano privacy-chain dollar token with limited public reserve detail and no Pharos-supported chain {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}}: visibility only, low confidence. Freedom Dollar is a Zano ecosystem dollar asset admitted through CoinGecko. Its privacy-chain context and unsupported chain mean Pharos cannot attach a contract or run reserve sync today. The reserve model is therefore a high-risk single slice based on ecosystem collateral and documented peg intent. With no independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} or verifiable {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} disclosures, FUSD remains visible in the dashboard while confidence is kept appropriately low.

fusd-finchain.title: A Rebasing Bermuda Dollar
fusd-finchain.text: FinChain Dollar is a BMA-licensed, {{term:yield-bearing}}rebasing{{/term}} dollar backed by tokenized U.S. Treasury bill and money-market fund products. The token targets a fixed $1 value while balances rebase daily, so the yield shows up as more FUSD rather than a rising NAV. DefiLlama provides the runtime price and supply path, while FinChain's own reserve dashboard and docs describe Taikang, ChinaAMC, and BNY Mellon/Finloop reserve assets. The main caveats are issuer concentration, eligible-customer access, and reserve transparency that is still issuer-led rather than a deeply integrated independent feed.

zsd-zephyr-protocol.title: The Zephyr Privacy Dollar
zsd-zephyr-protocol.text:
A Djed-inspired algorithmic dollar on Zephyr's Monero-derived private chain, minted against volatile native ZEPH with reserve-ratio constraints.

Zephyr Stable Dollar is a protocol-native private-chain stablecoin admitted through CoinGecko plus Zephyr Scanner telemetry rather than a supported Pharos contract path. Its Djed-inspired {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} design mints and redeems ZSD against ZEPH reserve collateral, with reserve-ratio constraints intended to preserve {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}}. Pharos sources ZSD supply and reserve ratio data from Zephyr's official API, but keeps the reserve slice high risk because the backing asset is volatile native ZEPH on an unsupported private chain.

zys-zephyr-protocol.title: The Zephyr Yield Share
zys-zephyr-protocol.text:
NAV-style yield-share wrapper over ZSD that inherits Zephyr's private-chain and ZEPH-collateral risk through its underlying reserve dependency.

Zephyr Yield Share is the NAV-style {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper for Zephyr's ZSD yield reserve, not the base stablecoin itself. ZYS supply, price, and APY come from Zephyr Scanner because CoinGecko and DefiLlama do not expose the wrapper as a market row. Pharos tracks it separately so yield is attributed to the actual yield-share token while base ZSD remains non-yield-bearing. The entry inherits Zephyr's private-chain and {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} ZEPH-collateral risk through its ZSD reserve dependency.

iusd-indigo-protocol.title: The Cardano Synthetic Dollar
iusd-indigo-protocol.text: Cardano-native synthetic dollar minted from overcollateralized Cardano-asset CDPs; Cardano supply remains curated rather than live-verified. Indigo iUSD is a Cardano synthetic dollar minted against overcollateralized positions in Indigo Protocol. Its risk profile is a classic crypto-CDP profile: collateral volatility, liquidation execution, oracle quality, and governance all matter. Pharos stores the Cardano asset identifier and DefiLlama provider ID, but Cardano supply is not yet live-verified. The reserve view stays curated until a Cardano-capable verification path exists. Risk is dominated by classic {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} dynamics: collateral volatility against the {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} ratio and the maturity of the {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} venue on Cardano.

cdp-enosys.title: Flare's CDP Experiment
cdp-enosys.text: CDP is Enosys Loans' Flare-native dollar, minted against FXRP, wFLR, sFLR, and stXRP vaults priced by the Flare Time Series Oracle. The mechanism is a Liquity V2 friendly fork: user-set borrow rates, a Stability Pool for liquidations, and redemptions against the lowest-rate positions when the market stops pretending one CDP is worth one dollar. That is a more interesting peg engine than another issuer IOU, but it still concentrates risk in Flare collateral depth, oracle assumptions, and Enosys governance parameters. Pharos treats the mint path as bounded by overcollateralized vault rules, while noting that the token proxy and risk settings still sit behind multisig and proxy-admin control. In other words, it is decentralized enough to be mechanically legible, not decentralized enough to make admin risk disappear.

luausd-lumi-finance.title: The Lumi Floor-Dollar
luausd-lumi-finance.text: NAV-style dollar reference token on Arbitrum tied to LUA floor-price mechanics; not a 1:1 redeemable fiat stablecoin. Lumi Finance LUAUSD is not a conventional 1:1 redeemable dollar. It is a dollar-referenced synthetic tied to LUA floor-price and protocol-owned liquidity mechanics, so Pharos marks it as NAV-style and high risk. The Arbitrum contract enables curated validation, but the reserve slice is intentionally broad because public proof is weak. This entry is included for provider coverage, with a warning that the stability claim is nonstandard. The peg claim is closer to an {{term:algorithmic}}algorithmic{{/term}} floor-price reference than fiat backing, and no documented {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} window or third-party {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} is currently modelled by Pharos.

susd-solayer.title: The Solana T-Bill Rebase
susd-solayer.text: Solayer sUSD is a Solana Token-2022 interest-bearing dollar whose balances grow from T-bill exposure rather than staying as a static par token. The structure is simple on paper: Solayer workflows handle minting, the interest extension handles balance growth, and the reserve model points to U.S. T-bill or RWA partner exposure. The risk is in the operational wrapper, because holder exits depend on issuer workflows, Solana token semantics, and institutional custody assumptions rather than a permissionless redemption contract. Pharos uses the Solana mint for curated reserve validation and keeps the reserve slice conservative until a stronger transparency feed exists. The float, meanwhile, has kept bleeding out with no public explanation. What circulates today is a residual balance measured in hundreds of thousands of dollars, the early-warning signal has drifted out of calm into watch, and the economic-control pillar sits at the bottom of the scale. The peg still reads perfect, which is the least reassuring kind of perfect. A T-bill wrapper nobody is left holding does not need to depeg to have failed.

usx-dforce.title: Overcollateralized on Paper
usx-dforce.text: dForce USD is now a read-only archive: Pharos froze USX on 2026-07-18 after it slid to roughly $0.39 with on-chain liquidity measured in tens of thousands of dollars and daily volume under $10. The {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style design launched in 2021 and peaked above $205M in mid-2022, but it never truly recovered from that bear market. Legacy debt positions on the dForce/Unitus lending protocol left circulating USX without a credible par-{{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} route, and the discount widened from cents to a chasm over four years. The terminal slide was orderly in the way glaciers are: below $0.75 in February 2026, below $0.45 by April, and near $0.39 by the July freeze, with the DF governance token near zero and no published remediation plan to point at. The epitaph writes itself: {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} on paper, unredeemable in practice. Collateral you cannot claim at par is balance-sheet decoration, not a backstop.

home-homecoin.title: The Property-Lien Dollar
home-homecoin.text: USD stablecoin backed by U.S. home-loan liens and property receivables; foreclosure is the recovery path, not redemption liquidity. HomeCoin is backed by U.S. home loan liens and property-backed receivables rather than cash, T-bills, or crypto collateral. That makes the asset interesting but illiquid: a foreclosure right is not the same thing as immediate redemption liquidity. Pharos tracks the Ethereum contract, self-reported collateral source, and DefiLlama provider entry while assigning high reserve risk. The real-estate lending model is documented in metadata, but HOME is not classified as yield-bearing until a holder-level yield source is verified. Reserve risk is dominated by mortgage-lien {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} quality rather than cash {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path runs through loan workouts, not an issuer window. The market has started pricing that structure honestly: the one thin pool where HOME trades currently marks it at a double-digit discount to par.

cdxusd-cod3x.title: The Facilitator-Minted Dollar
cdxusd-cod3x.text: cdxUSD is Cod3x's Base stablecoin minted by permissioned Facilitators against strategy-managed collateral; risk concentrates in those mint permissions. Cod3x USD is a Base stablecoin minted by protocol Facilitators under configured limits and strategies. The model can be powerful, but it also concentrates risk in facilitator permissions, collateral management, and strategy transparency. Pharos adds the Base contract and uses a single high-risk reserve slice until the backing is more granular. Its {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} backstop is documented at the mechanism level, not scored as a liquid public route. Facilitator-managed minting resembles a permissioned {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} variant rather than a public {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}}.

susd-hedgecore.title: The Soul-Bound USDC Yield Token
susd-hedgecore.text: HedgeCore SUSD is a BSC yield wrapper minted from USDC and routed through Venus lending, with soul-bound behavior doing the opposite of what most stablecoin holders expect from a dollar token. The reserve dependency is explicit: USDC enters HedgeCore's strategy layer, earns through Venus, and gets reflected back through operator-mediated reward and exit mechanics. Pharos marks it yield-bearing but keeps the APY source conservative because a reliable public pool feed is not part of the current data path. The real warning is mobility, not collateral naming: early redemption is operator-controlled and the hUSDC wrapper only opens one direction. SUSD may be stable in accounting terms, but the exit door has a staff member standing in front of it.

usd3-reserve-protocol.title: The Reserve Basket Dollar
usd3-reserve-protocol.text: USD3 is a Reserve Protocol RToken/DTF that turns yield-bearing wrappers into a dollar basket, which is clever until you count the upstream assumptions. The backing is split across Savings USDS, Aave USDC, wrapped Compound USDCv3, and Steakhouse USDC strategy exposure, so holders are buying a governed portfolio of stablecoin yield rather than a single clean reserve. Reserve's real-time protocol feed and basket redemption mechanics make the structure more inspectable than most wrapper stacks. RSR stakers and governance absorb and manage losses, but that also means parameter choices and collateral onboarding matter as much as the assets themselves. USD3 is a tidy DeFi balance-sheet product; the sardonic bit is that its simplicity ends exactly where the basket begins.

sofid-sofi.title: The Fed's Own Stablecoin Customer
sofid-sofi.text: SoFiUSD is what happens when a nationally chartered U.S. bank decides the stablecoin wrapper is worth adding to old-fashioned cash at the Federal Reserve. Reserves sit at SoFi Bank's Fed master account, with BitGo running 1:1 mint and redemption on an upgradeable, bank-controlled contract. The distribution question got its answer in May 2026, when SoFi opened the token to its nearly 15 million app members, making SOFID the first national-bank stablecoin offered directly inside a consumer banking app. What has not arrived is a number: no permitted market-data source reports a positive circulating supply or market cap, so Pharos has temporarily withheld the listing until the figures exist. The attestation story is similarly aspirational. Press coverage mentions monthly Deloitte verification, but no public attestation report or transparency page has materialized. A bank that can put a stablecoin in front of fifteen million customers but not a supply figure in front of anyone is running bank-grade issuance with bank-grade opacity, and only one of those is a compliment.

sources.label: SoFi press release: SoFiUSD retail launch to nearly 15M members (May 27, 2026)

usdb-bridge.title: Stripe Bridge USDB Payments Rail
usdb-bridge.text: Bridge's USDB is Stripe's invisible stablecoin rail, with reserves at BlackRock {{term:money-market-fund}}MMFs{{/term}} under an OCC trust charter and distribution embedded in $1T of annual payment flow. USDB is the stablecoin most people will never know they're using. Bridge, Stripe's $1.1 billion acquisition, quietly powers Stablecoin Financial Accounts in 101 countries, turning every Stripe merchant into a potential stablecoin endpoint without the merchant ever touching a token. The OCC conditional national trust bank charter from February 2026 gives Bridge the federal regulatory cover that most stablecoin issuers spend years pursuing, and the reserves sit in cash and BlackRock money market funds with institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}. USDB's strategic value comes from Stripe processing $1 trillion annually. The company can embed stablecoin settlement into existing payment flows without asking permission from anyone downstream.
