The competitive moat is distribution through indifference rather than technology or regulation.

hkdap-anchorpoint.title: The Proof Nobody Checks
hkdap-anchorpoint.text: The first HKMA-licensed HKD stablecoin under the Stablecoins Ordinance, now live in an institution-only beta and finally measurable. After two missed launch windows, HKDAP went out on August 12 2026 attested by its distributors rather than its issuer. OSL Group and HashKey Exchange announced themselves as authorised, while anchorpoint.hk read "has not yet officially launched." DefiLlama picked the token up on August 27, and the Ethereum deployment carries roughly 527,000 HKDAP, so supply is now independently verifiable. On August 14 BlockSec published a review of that same contract: the KYC proof argument is passed in and then discarded, so any proof, including an empty string, passes; de-registering a compromised KYC provider does not stop the wallets it onboarded from transacting; a single key can mint, burn, pause, or freeze, with two keys controlling every upgrade and role and no timelocks or multi-signature anywhere on the high-risk path. Debug logging left in the proxy fallback, an optimizer set to zero runs, and test files uploaded to Etherscan point to a pre-production build sitting on mainnet. The regulator vetted the issuer, not the bytecode. Pharos still holds HKDAP pre-launch, though the reason has changed: supply is no longer missing; price is, with DefiLlama reporting null and CoinGecko carrying a preview listing with no market data. The licensing playbook rests on segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, HKMA-mandated {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and a regulated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path scoped for HKD-denominated {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} settlement. None of this is enforced by the contract that actually moves the tokens.

hkd-hsbc.title: PayMe Gets a Blockchain
hkd-hsbc.text: HSBC's HKMA-licensed HKD stablecoin (pre-launch, H2 2026) leveraging 3.3M PayMe users as its distribution moat. HSBC's HKD stablecoin is the second HKMA-licensed entry and the one with the distribution advantage that matters: 3.3 million PayMe users who already use the app for peer-to-peer payments and won't need to download anything new. The integration into HSBC's HK App for tokenized investment subscriptions points to the actual product thesis. HSBC is building a settlement layer for its own digital asset products, with standalone DeFi as a secondary use case. H2 2026 is the target, the reserves will be HKD-denominated high-quality liquid assets in segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} accounts per HKMA rules with HKMA-mandated {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} routed through PayMe and the HSBC HK app, and the symbol hasn't even been confirmed yet. The interesting tension: HSBC is building a stablecoin specifically to avoid depending on anyone else's stablecoin, which is either strategic autonomy or institutional NIH syndrome depending on your perspective.

okrw-hashed.title: Korea Builds Its Own Chain
okrw-hashed.text: Pre-launch native KRW stablecoin of Maroo, Hashed Open Finance's sovereign L1 testnet built specifically for Korean Won; regulated and open issuance tracks, mainnet targeted for late 2026. Hashed Open Finance built a KRW stablecoin on an entire Layer 1 blockchain designed to host it. Maroo is positioned as the first 'sovereign L1' purpose-built for Korean Won stablecoins, with a dual-track design that offers both a regulated path (bank-backed, KYC-gated) and an open path (permissionless issuance). The testnet went live in May 2026 with OKRW as the native token, and mainnet is targeted before year-end. In a country where crypto trading volumes regularly rival the stock market but regulated stablecoin infrastructure is virtually nonexistent, the thesis is less about technology and more about regulatory positioning: whoever builds the compliant KRW on-ramp first captures a market that has been using USDT as a proxy currency by default.

arc-anq.title: The Rupee's On-Chain Debut
arc-anq.text: ARC is a pre-launch INR stablecoin from Anq, designed for a regulated 1:1 rupee peg backed by cash, fixed deposits, and Indian government securities. ARC is India's first attempt at a regulated rupee stablecoin, built by Anq with Polygon's backing and designed to prevent the USD liquidity outflow that India's regulators have been panicking about since USDT volumes on Indian exchanges started dwarfing domestic payment rail throughput. The collateral is cash, fixed deposits, and Indian government securities. It reads like a mutual fund prospectus, with {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} at regulated Indian banks, and the two-tier framework is explicitly designed to complement rather than compete with the RBI's digital rupee CBDC. The Uniswap v4 whitelisting for compliance is a novel technical approach to the 'permissioned token on a permissionless chain' problem, and primary {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} will run through KYC-gated issuer rails rather than open market making. Whether India's regulatory apparatus will actually let a private rupee stablecoin operate alongside its CBDC remains the existential question that no amount of technical architecture can answer.

brl-b3.title: The Stock Exchange Mints Money
brl-b3.text: BRL-B3 is a pre-launch Brazilian real settlement stablecoin from B3, Latin America's largest stock exchange, designed for its tokenized {{term:rwa}}real-world-asset{{/term}} trading platform. When Latin America's largest stock exchange decides it needs its own stablecoin for tokenized asset settlement, the signal is less about crypto adoption and more about what traditional financial infrastructure considers table stakes in 2026. B3's BRL stablecoin is branded B3RL, built on Polygon, and backed by cash and government bonds inside B3's own clearing infrastructure. It fills the gap left by Brazil's Drex CBDC narrowing its scope: the central bank's digital currency was meant to handle settlement, but as that project slowed, B3 decided to build the settlement rails itself. The timeline has moved: the first-half-of-2026 window floated at May's Tokenization Day has come and gone, and by July's Expert XP conference the line had softened to a launch 'in the coming months,' with asset tokenization itself pushed to early 2027. B3 clears trillions annually. The open questions are whether Brazil's regulators will let a stock exchange run the settlement rails the central bank once reserved for itself and whether 'coming months' survives contact with the CVM.

usdf-flipcash.title: Coinbase's White-Label Dollar
usdf-flipcash.text: Flipcash's USDF is the first Coinbase Custom Stablecoin, a USDC wrapper used to prove out the stablecoin-as-a-service platform. USDF is the first stablecoin minted through Coinbase's Custom Stablecoins platform, a stablecoin-as-a-service product that lets any business launch a branded dollar backed 1:1 by USDC. Flipcash is the guinea pig, and the product itself is less interesting than the platform it proves out: if Custom Stablecoins works, every fintech, neobank, and loyalty program can have its own branded dollar without touching reserve management. The dependency chain is explicit: USDF is a wrapper around USDC, which is a wrapper around BlackRock-managed {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}. Governance is centralized-dependent because the token's existence depends on Coinbase continuing to operate the platform. Whether the world needs branded USDC wrappers or whether this is just a new distribution strategy for Circle's existing product is a question Coinbase would prefer you didn't ask too loudly.

krw-imbank.title: Quantum-Resistant Won
krw-imbank.text: Korean commercial-bank KRW PoC on Kaia with post-quantum security; symbolic of regulatory thaw rather than a commercial product. iM Bank's KRW stablecoin proof-of-concept has a feature that most stablecoins won't need for a decade but makes excellent press releases: quantum-resistant post-quantum cryptography via BTQ Technologies on the Kaia blockchain. Set aside the security theater angle, and the actual significance is that a Korean commercial bank is building a KRW stablecoin at all. South Korea's regulatory stance on private stablecoins has been cautious to the point of paralysis, and a bank-led PoC signals that the regulatory ice may be thawing. The Finger partnership handles the wallet and DeFi integration layer, while iM Bank brings the banking license and the KRW reserves. Whether this moves beyond proof-of-concept depends entirely on whether Korean regulators want to compete with Hashed's OKRW for the title of first regulated KRW stablecoin or whether they'd prefer neither existed. As a bank-issued PoC, the stack assumes regulated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} of KRW reserves, statutory {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, and a banking-rail {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} path that has yet to face commercial traffic.

gldy-streamex.title: The Yield-Bearing Gold Ounce
gldy-streamex.text: GLDY is Streamex's {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} tokenized gold ounce on Base, with Chainlink Proof of Reserve and gold-leasing receivables as the source of returns. Streamex GLDY tracks one troy ounce of gold while passing gold-leasing yield back to token holders. The entry is stronger than most new commodity tokens because it has a Chainlink proof-of-reserves feed on Base and a documented primary-market {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} route for eligible investors. The main caveat is that the yield comes from issuer-managed gold leasing rather than passive vault storage, so Pharos separates the live reserve feed from the not-yet-integrated APY source. Distribution is being built with unusual seriousness for a token this young. It has 24/7 secondary liquidity infrastructure with Orca, followed by a June brokerage-channel deal routing GLDY through Siebert's wealth-management desks with tZERO. GLDY is tracked as a commodity stablecoin, not as a generic RWA fund.

vnxau-vnx.title: The Liechtenstein Gram-Gold Token
vnxau-vnx.text: VNX Gold represents one gram of physical gold under Liechtenstein's regulated-issuer pattern, with AREVA reserve reports and Ethereum supply tracking. VNX Gold represents one gram of physical gold and fits the same regulated-issuer pattern as VNX's fiat stablecoins. AREVA reserve reports and {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}-style VNX documentation give enough backing detail to track the token, while the Ethereum supply probe provides lightweight live sync until a stronger public reserve API is available. Redemption is meaningful but operationally constrained: verified platform users can sell or request physical delivery from larger bar denominations. The risk is less the gold unit and more the issuer, custody, and platform access path.

xagm-matrixdock.title: Matrixdock's Silver Ounce
xagm-matrixdock.text: Matrixdock's silver token finally entered the Bureau Veritas programme this year. XAGm's first inclusion involved a full physical count of 66 Good Delivery bars against the parcel ownership list, with no anomalies. It cost the token its reserve composition anyway. The certificate examines the vault as of the end of June, and Pharos now dates composition to when the work was done rather than when the PDF was posted, which lands XAGm a little over a week outside the 31-day freshness window; the single silver row drops out of scoring and backing falls far enough to take the grade to F. The count also exposes the deeper gap: XAGm tokens appear nowhere in the certificate. This is assets-only physical inventory: an inspection of metal with no reconciliation to what has been issued against it. It is paired with a mint path the authority review reads as unbounded, since an operator can top up local mint budget without any reserve-side check. The bars are real; the arithmetic connecting them to your token remains entirely the issuer's to assert.

gramg-token-teknoloji.title: Turkey's Gram-Gold Token
gramg-token-teknoloji.text: GRAMG is Token Teknoloji's one-gram gold claim from Turkey, and the open question is what, exactly, sits behind it: the issuer's product copy says equivalent PAXG is held on-chain, while the same page's FAQ and reserve disclosures describe physical gold at Turkish banks, the Central Bank, and company vaults. No current primary evidence reconciles the two stories. The reserve proof page does not help its own case: the supply widget renders empty, the evidence link points at an Ethereum address while the copy talks about Avalanche, and there is no independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, only the issuer's word at self-reported tier. {{term:redemption}}Redemption{{/term}} remains unscored because no reviewed direct-holder schedule has ever been published. Since mid-July 2026 the coin has been quarantined on Pharos because no permitted runtime source reports a positive circulating supply or market cap. It is a gold token whose backing form is disputed and whose token count is unverifiable. A gram of something is presumably somewhere; the disclosures cannot agree on what, and the data cannot confirm how much.

grams-token-teknoloji.title: Turkey's Gram-Silver Token
grams-token-teknoloji.text: GRAMS is Token Teknoloji's one-gram silver claim, the sibling of its gold product, with proof pages naming physical silver at Kuveyt Türk, VakıfBank, Ziraat Participation, and Akbank. The disclosure is at least consistently inconsistent: the product page describes company-vault {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} while the shared proof-of-reserves page names the banks, the reserve page reuses the gold token's contract address, and leftover platinum copy suggests the whole thing was assembled by find-and-replace. There is no independent {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}. The live feed Pharos wires up reads token supply on Avalanche, which proves the token exists, not that the silver does. {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} stays unmodeled because no direct-holder terms are documented. Since mid-July 2026 the coin has been quarantined on Pharos: no permitted runtime source reports a positive circulating supply or market cap. Somewhere in a Turkish vault there may be silver by the gram; the evidence trail stops several steps short of it.

euroe-membrane.title: Redemption-Only EUROe
euroe-membrane.text: EUROe is now best read in the past tense, which is not where a growth stablecoin wants to live. Membrane's Finnish EMI-licensed euro token has moved into Paxos' redemption-only wind-down after the product line was decommissioned, leaving holders with a 1:1 EUR exit path rather than an expanding on-chain euro network. The old reserve story was straightforward euro fiat and euro-denominated assets, but the current proof source is a redemption notice, not an ongoing reserve machine. Pharos still records the multichain contracts and regulated-entity posture, while the mint authority history shows EOA admin control and no heroic decentralization epilogue. EUROe's lesson is blunt: regulatory seriousness can make wind-down orderly, but it cannot make a discontinued token relevant.

gbpm-mento.title: Mento's CDP Pound
gbpm-mento.text: GBPm is Mento's British pound stablecoin on Celo, minted from {{term:cdp}}CDPs{{/term}} collateralized by USDm with oracle-priced {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}. GBPm extends Mento's Celo FX stablecoin set into sterling using USDm-collateralized CDP rows rather than the older shared reserve basket alone. Mento's dashboard API exposes GBPm troves, turning live collateral and debt into visible reserve evidence. That makes the entry useful despite a modest supply footprint because the backing path is visible and cheap to maintain. The primary risk is dependency on Mento oracles, Celo execution, and USDm collateral quality.

jpym-mento.title: Mento's CDP Yen
jpym-mento.text: Small CDP yen on Celo backed by USDm collateral via Mento troves; CoinGecko-admitted, Mento API exposes live CDP collateral. JPYm is a small but active yen stablecoin on Celo, backed by USDm collateral in Mento CDP troves. Pharos uses CoinGecko admission because DefiLlama's JPYm supply row is zero, while the Mento API still exposes live CDP collateral. The Mento API keeps reserve visibility aligned with GBPm and CHFm. JPYm is tracked for strategic non-USD coverage, with liquidity and oracle dependency as the main caveats. As a Mento FX stablecoin, JPYm rests on a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} with USDm {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} and oracle-priced FPMM swaps acting as the {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} surface against the reserve.

chfm-mento.title: Mento's CDP Franc
chfm-mento.text: CHFm is a Mento CDP-backed Swiss franc stablecoin on Celo, minted against USDm collateral rather than fiat reserves. CHFm gives Pharos another Swiss-franc stablecoin, but with a very different risk profile from fiat-backed VCHF or Frankencoin. Its reserves are USDm collateral posted into Mento {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} troves, and Mento live data exposes those rows directly. The asset is small, but the backing path is visible enough for reserve tracking. The residual risks are the Celo/Mento mechanism, USDm collateral path, and thin secondary liquidity. {{term:overcollateralization}}Overcollateralization{{/term}} and {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} logic inside Mento drive peg maintenance.

bfusd-binance.title: Binance's Account Dollar
bfusd-binance.text: BFUSD is a Binance account product redeemable inside Binance against USD stablecoins, backed by a {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-hedged{{/term}} collateral pool, staked crypto, and a reserve fund, all legally and beneficially owned by Binance, leaving holders with product terms rather than claims. It was originally tracked for its CoinGecko coverage and large Binance user footprint, but {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} runs entirely through Binance-controlled terms that permit fees, limits, delays, and outright suspension, with self-reported, ad-hoc disclosures standing in for independent proof of reserves. Pharos delisted the entry in July 2026 as out of scope: BFUSD is a non-withdrawable account balance rather than a transferable production token, so there is no on-chain supply to measure and no independent {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} to verify. The strategy behind it may well be run competently: the point is that nobody outside Binance can check. A dollar you cannot withdraw, transfer, or audit is less a stablecoin than a database row with an APR.

pathusd-bridge.title: Tempo's Bridge Dollar
pathusd-bridge.text: Bridge-issued dollar quote token for Tempo, backed by institutional reserves and redeemable through Bridge-supported flows; matters more as a payment-chain rail than for current scale. pathUSD is the Bridge-issued dollar quote token for Tempo, backed by a conventional reserve portfolio and redeemable back through Bridge-supported {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} flows. The asset matters less because of current scale than because it is native to a payment-focused chain that may become an important stablecoin rail. The risk profile is straightforward: institutional reserve assets and issuer redemption on the strong side, new-chain execution and limited independent reserve telemetry on the weak side.

djed-coti.title: Cardano's Reserve-Coin Stable
djed-coti.text: DJED is Cardano's formally designed reserve-coin stablecoin, not a borrower CDP wearing a different hat. ADA sits in the reserve, DJED is the dollar claim, and SHEN absorbs surplus and volatility inside the protocol's 400% to 800% reserve-ratio band. That design gives the peg a clear mechanical buffer, but it also ties the whole system to ADA collateral risk and to the COTI/IOG oracle role. The minting policy is materially constrained by Cardano smart-contract rules rather than a discretionary issuer desk, which is a real structural virtue. DJED is one of the cleaner algorithmic-adjacent designs, though crypto has earned the right to treat every reserve-coin elegance proof as an invitation to ask what happens when the reserve asset has a bad month.

usdv-solomon.title: The Ceffu Strategy Dollar
usdv-solomon.text: Solomon's USDv is a Solana stablecoin backed by Ceffu-custodied {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} margin, with aggregate disclosure but no live composition feed and no documented holder redemption path. Solomon USDv is a Solana stablecoin backed by Ceffu-custodied strategy assets and off-exchange {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} margin via {{term:basis-trade}}basis trade{{/term}} positions. The public supply is easy to validate on-chain, but the reserve disclosure is aggregate and does not expose a live composition API. That keeps the Pharos entry conservative: useful for tracking a visible Solana dollar, but not a high-confidence reserve model. Without a documented holder {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} route and with all collateral sitting in Ceffu {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, the backstop remains intentionally unmodeled.

fxd-fathom.title: XDC's Native CDP Dollar
fxd-fathom.text: FXD is Fathom's {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-minted dollar on XDC, {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} by XDC and stabilized by {{term:liquidation}}liquidations{{/term}} plus a stability module. Fathom Dollar gives the XDC ecosystem a native overcollateralized dollar backed by XDC and Fathom collateral-pool positions. It is tracked for chain coverage and DefiLlama visibility despite modest scale. The design is a familiar CDP mechanism: mint against collateral, burn to repay, liquidate weak positions, and use a stability module for peg support, but the collateral base and chain liquidity make it materially riskier than larger Ethereum CDP systems.

usp-pareto-credit.title: Private Credit With a Dollar Wrapper
usp-pareto-credit.text: Pareto USP was a dollar token whose reserve stack was mostly Pareto private-credit vault exposure, with small USDC and USDS buffers doing the polite work of pretending liquidity was simple. Verified users could mint and redeem through Pareto while open-market holders relied on secondary liquidity. This access split was always the product's central tension, because private credit never had the exit profile of cash, T-bills, or a permissionless collateral redemption path. The market priced that mismatch first, as a soft depeg that never fully closed, and then stopped pricing it at all: by mid-July 2026 the CoinGecko feed had gone stale around $0.85 with daily volume measured in single-digit dollars. Pharos had already moved USP onto a relaxed low-volume pricing fallback; when even that path failed, tracking was terminated on 2026-07-19 alongside a batch of other unpriceable assets. It was not frozen or cemeteried; it simply became no longer measurable. A credit product with a dollar ticker can survive many things, but a dashboard cannot track a price the market has stopped quoting.

dllr-sovryn.title: Rootstock's Mynt Basket
dllr-sovryn.text: DLLR is Sovryn's BTC-backed dollar basket on Rootstock; reserves are other CDP stables (ZUSD-dominated), readable on-chain. DLLR is Sovryn's Rootstock dollar basket, currently dominated by ZUSD with a small DOC position. The reserve holder can be read on-chain, and the Mynt {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} route maps naturally to a basket backstop. The residual risk is not opaque {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, but concentration in Rootstock liquidity, Sovryn governance, and the quality of the underlying BTC-backed stablecoins. Underlying bAssets are themselves {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoins with {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} against rBTC.

xusd-babelfish.title: The Rootstock Stablecoin Basket
xusd-babelfish.text:
A Rootstock basket dollar minted 1:1 from bridged stablecoins. It offers a basket exit route rather than a fiat-issuer promise, with recursive bridge and dependency risk.

XUSD is BabelFish's Rootstock basket stablecoin, backed by DLLR plus {{term:bridge}}bridged{{/term}} USDT, USDC, DAI, DOC, and related bAssets, with mint and redeem flowing through a basket-level {{term:psm}}PSM-style{{/term}} module. Pharos tracks live branch balances directly from the basket holder and links the largest dependency back to the newly tracked DLLR entry. The model is useful but recursive: XUSD inherits the risks of Rootstock {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} liquidity, DLLR's own basket, and BabelFish's balancing fees. It is a basket exit route, not a fiat issuer promise.

susdd-tron-dao-reserve.title: Savings USDD Wrapper
susdd-tron-dao-reserve.text: sUSDD is a savings wrapper over USDD, which means the first analytical move is not to invent a new peg mechanism. Users deposit USDD, receive a wrapper whose exchange rate appreciates, and ultimately inherit USDD's reserve, PSM, and redemption assumptions on the way out. The wrapper contract itself is comparatively clean, with immutable DSR-style mechanics and no owner or proxy, but the base asset below it is still the load-bearing risk. Pharos records self-reported real-time USDD data, which is useful without being independent reserve assurance. sUSDD is yield passthrough, not alchemy; the wrapper may be tidy, but it cannot launder the parent coin's risk into a different species.

onyc-onre.title: The Reinsurance NAV Token
onyc-onre.text: ONYC is a Solana NAV token tied to OnRe-managed structured insurance and reinsurance yield, not a plain $1 payment stablecoin with cash in a bank account. Its value is meant to accrue from insurance-market collateral returns, with Apex Group audit coverage and OnRe's Bermuda licensing providing the institutional wrapper. The portfolio is still a single high-risk reserve slice in Pharos because structured reinsurance is not exactly a T-bill ladder with a friendly UI. Primary access remains governed by OnRe's platform terms, and the mint surface runs through an upgradeable Solana program controlled by the issuer. The pitch is yield from a genuinely different real-world market; the catch is that every exit still depends on a high-touch issuer process.

apyusd-apyx.title: Apyx Savings Share
apyusd-apyx.text: apyUSD is a savings wrapper over apxUSD that turns Apyx's preferred-share collateral into a rising NAV. It is not a cash layer. The parent reserve stack is the interesting part: Digital Asset Treasury preferred equity and liquidity buffers sit underneath, which is a long way from a plain Treasury-bill stablecoin. In June 2026 that collateral thesis got its real-work moment and failed it: apxUSD followed Strategy's preferred stock below par and still trades under the dollar, so the wrapper's failing card is mostly inherited arithmetic: an ERC-4626 share can compound yield all it likes, but it compounds on top of whatever the parent is actually worth. Pharos treats the Accountable feed as useful live proof for the wrapper while still carrying the parent dependency and the concentrated Apyx admin surface forward: the latter now graded as a failing economic-control pillar in its own right. A savings share is only as good as the thing being saved.

susd1plus-lorenzo.title: Lorenzo Strategy Dollar
susd1plus-lorenzo.text: Lorenzo's staked receipt over the USD1+ strategy dollar, blending WLFI USD1 reserve yield with delta-neutral CEX strategies on BNB Chain. sUSD1+ adds Lorenzo Protocol exposure to the USD1-linked strategy-dollar family. The wrapper is {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}}, with returns sourced from {{term:delta-neutral}}delta-neutral{{/term}} {{term:basis-trade}}basis trade{{/term}} positions and CEX strategy access driven by {{term:funding-rate}}funding rate{{/term}} dynamics. Public data supports metadata and supply tracking, but the reserve and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} mechanics are less transparent than the cleaner ERC-4626 wrappers, so the entry carries exotic collateral and CEX-strategy {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} risk.

savusd-avant.title: Avant Staked Dollar
savusd-avant.text: savUSD is Avant's staked avUSD receipt, with the exchange rate rising as the senior tranche earns from actively managed market-neutral strategies. The protection stack is explicit but not magical: Avant points to a Reserve Fund and junior avUSDx tranche before savUSD takes losses, while Pennyworks supplies the weekly NAV calculation. Unstaking has a one-day cooldown with no yield, and the final exit still inherits avUSD's 1:1 USDC redemption process. Pharos therefore reads savUSD as a yield sleeve over a managed strategy book, not as a faster or safer dollar than its parent.

steakusdc-steakhouse.title: Circle, With Borrowers
steakusdc-steakhouse.text: Steakhouse USDC is an immutable MetaMorpho vault share over USDC, so the base dollar is Circle's but the yield comes from borrowers in Steakhouse-curated Morpho markets. That distinction matters: the vault does not improve Circle's reserve story, it adds curator choices, lending collateral, and withdrawal liquidity on top of it. Pharos treats the wrapper minting as deposit-only share accounting while inheriting the underlying USDC issuer risk and tracking the Steakhouse governance surface separately. It is a clean-looking USDC yield wrapper, but exits still depend on available Morpho liquidity; the word "instant" is doing some reputational heavy lifting.

bbqusdc-steakhouse.title: Smokehouse's Higher-Risk USDC Vault
bbqusdc-steakhouse.text: Smokehouse USDC is Steakhouse's high-yield MetaMorpho vault over USDC, built for borrowers and collateral types that sit outside the calmer Prime line, tokenized private-credit style markets included. The wrapper itself uses a clear mechanism: an immutable ERC-4626 vault, shares minted only against deposits, a Steakhouse multisig that can steer allocations but cannot conjure base dollars. No evidence showed that anyone supervises or reconciles that mint, and this release stopped extending credit for the claim; economic control drops to the floor reserved for minting nobody independently checks, and a card that read A- now reads D. Be precise about what did not happen: the collateral did not move, the USDC underneath it scores exactly as it did last month, and exit remains one of the stronger pillars on any wrapper Pharos tracks. This is a single-pillar downgrade on a documentation gap, and it is also the first time Pharos has scored the Smokehouse sleeve at the risk level its own name advertises: exotic collateral, curator discretion, and an exit that depends on Morpho markets unwinding faster than depositors change their minds.

srusde-strata.title: Senior, Not Simple
srusde-strata.text: srUSDe is Strata's senior ERC-4626 tranche over a strategy that stakes USDe into Ethena's yield stack, with jrUSDe taking first-loss before senior holders are touched. The tranche structure gives senior capital a subordination buffer and a benchmark-rate yield floor. The discipline argument aged badly in July 2026, when Lido's EarnUSD vault began allocating to PT-srUSDe, the fixed-rate claim on this very tranche, looped on Aave with leverage extended through Twyne. The naked leveraged loop that tranching was supposed to replace has simply been rebuilt one layer up, with the senior tranche as its collateral. It is still not a plain dollar: exits depend on Strata tranche liquidity and settlement rules rather than 1:1 issuer redemption, which is why the exit pillar is the failing grade on an otherwise respectable backing score. The senior wrapper still inherits Ethena's liquid-stablecoin, BTC, ETH/LST, CEX-hedge, and custody assumptions; the junior tranche absorbs the first bruise, but if the machinery breaks badly enough, senior status becomes an adjective, not armor.

sources.label: CryptoBriefing: EarnUSD strategy loops PT-srUSDe on Aave via Twyne (July 22, 2026)

syzusd-yuzu.title: Yuzu Staked Wrapper
syzusd-yuzu.text: syzUSD is the staked wrapper for Yuzu USD, so its dollar story begins one layer below the token you are looking at. The wrapper appreciates against yzUSD as curated DeFi strategies accrue yield across Plasma and Monad, while exits inherit Yuzu's KYC-gated redemption and liquidity-buffer constraints. Accountable's real-time reserve feed is the right transparency surface, but Pharos keeps the wrapper identity separate so the same underlying risk is not double-counted as fresh backing. That distinction matters because syzUSD holders are taking strategy-vault risk, parent-coin risk, and young-chain deployment risk in one neat receipt. It is a yield wrapper with accounting discipline; whether that is enough depends on how much comfort one takes from transparent complexity.

fxsave-f-x-protocol.title: f(x) Stability Vault
fxsave-f-x-protocol.text: fxSAVE is an auto-compounding ERC-4626 receipt over f(x) Protocol's Stability Pool, not a simple parked fxUSD balance. The exit path runs through fxSP into a fxUSD-and-USDC mix, then onward into fxUSD's CDP machinery backed by WBTC and wstETH. That gives holders strategy yield and peg-support exposure in one package, but it also imports oracle, liquidation, Curve-pool, and governance-tuned collateral risk. Pharos classifies it as a high-risk NAV strategy vault because the wrapper may look like savings, while the engine underneath is still a leveraged crypto collateral system with better manners.

steakusdt-steakhouse.title: Steakhouse USDT Lending Vault
steakusdt-steakhouse.text: Steakhouse USDT is a MetaMorpho vault share over USDT, not a new dollar. Yield comes from borrower interest in Steakhouse-curated lending markets. The trust stack is Tether first, Morpho market liquidity second, and Steakhouse curator discipline third, which is quite a lot to fit inside one polite vault receipt. Pharos keeps the Tether issuer and blacklist dependency attached while separately treating the wrapper as a lending vault whose withdrawals rely on available USDT liquidity or patiently returning market capacity. It is a usable yield sleeve, but not a redemption backstop with a steak knife.

susn-noon.title: Noon's Yield Receipt
susn-noon.text: sUSN is the staked savings form of Noon USN, so its NAV appreciates while base USN remains the non-yielding settlement token. The wrapper inherits a reserve mix that is far busier than the name suggests: private credit, CLO exposure, DeFi lending, principal tokens, and a small Treasury-bill sleeve, with Accountable providing a real-time proof feed. That makes sUSN a yield receipt over a credit portfolio, not a fresh $1 stablecoin with its own clean redemption promise. Pharos tracks it separately because wrapper supply, NAV, and liquidity can diverge from liquid USN even though final exits still route through Noon whitelisting and USN reserve constraints. The nice part is transparent wrapper accounting; the less nice part is discovering how many doors sit between savings yield and cash.

mre7yield-midas.title: Midas Re7 Yield Token
mre7yield-midas.text: mRe7YIELD is a Midas and Re7 Capital liquid-yield token, with NAV appreciation sourced from DeFi lending, liquidity provision, restaking, funding-rate trades, and options strategies. That mix may be institutionally packaged, but it is not a cash reserve and should not be mistaken for one because the symbol has a dollar reference. Pharos gives credit for the daily Midas transparency feed while flagging the missing granular strategy-composition feed and the concentrated Midas mint/admin surface. It is a managed strategy note wearing stablecoin colors; useful for yield analytics, awkward as a transactional dollar.

hbusdt-hyperbeat.title: Hyperbeat USDT Vault
hbusdt-hyperbeat.text: hbUSDT is a HyperEVM vault share over USDT strategy exposure, not a cleaner version of Tether with a new logo. Pharos models the reserves as a split between hoUSDT strategy exposure and masterUSD strategy exposure, both high-risk, with Accountable providing real-time visibility that is helpful but still product-scope dependent. The parent leg inherits USDT and USDT0 risk, including Tether redemption discretion and cross-chain settlement assumptions, while the wrapper adds Hyperbeat vault liquidity, strategy allocation, and single-chain HyperEVM execution risk. It is yield-bearing because more machinery was inserted between the holder and the dollar, which is the stablecoin market's favorite magic trick.

witry-brix.title: Wrapped Turkish Lira Yield
witry-brix.text: wiTRY is a Brix staking wrapper over iTRY, exposing holders to a BVI-regulated TRY money-market fund and local Turkish-lira instruments. wiTRY brings a TRY-pegged {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} wrapper into the catalog. The Ethereum wrapper can be verified on-chain, while the underlying iTRY reserve and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} process remain more issuer-dependent than the mature fiat stablecoin set. The underlying iTRY exposure points at a BVI-regulated TRY money-market structure and local-currency instruments, which Pharos treats as {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} collateral with high jurisdictional and operational risk for a thinly traded TRY product.

srusd-reservoir.title: Reservoir Savings Token
srusd-reservoir.text: srUSD is Reservoir's savings wrapper over rUSD, so the immediate asset is a yield-accruing share and the underlying risk is the Reservoir balance sheet. That balance sheet is not a sleepy cash account: it includes stablecoin PSM liquidity, RWA allocations, Morpho and Euler lending vaults, and governance-approved credit strategies. The wrapper adds exchange-rate and exit-to-rUSD mechanics, while rUSD itself still depends on PSM liquidity and protocol risk controls for the actual stablecoin exit. Reservoir's real-time reserve endpoint gives Pharos a live window into the stack, but the window looks into a mixed credit book, not a vault of crisp bills.

usdn-smardex.title: Delta-Neutral USDN
usdn-smardex.text: SMARDEX USDN is the Ethereum synthetic dollar built around a wstETH-backed vault and delta-neutral protocol mechanics, not Noble USDN and blessedly not Neutrino nostalgia. Users mint and redeem through the vault, but the process can be throttled by protocol imbalance and a two-step oracle validation flow, so the peg mechanism is more state machine than cashier window. The token also rebases, which turns yield into a protocol accounting event rather than a separate savings wrapper. Pharos flags the bounded-but-permissioned mint path through the USDN vault and its 2-of-3 governance Safe, because elegant delta-neutral math still needs someone to hold the keys.

scusd-rings.title: Rings Stable Collateral
scusd-rings.text: Rings scUSD is the liquid scAsset, not the main savings wrapper, which is the first useful guardrail before anyone starts annualizing the wrong thing. The collateral model accepts stablecoins and routes a strategy sleeve through Trevee/Veda BoringVault infrastructure into venues such as Aave and Morpho, so the backing is part cash-like collateral and part curated DeFi exposure. Proof is still self-reported through published backing addresses, with Pharos carrying an explicit notice that deeper on-chain reserve tracking is pending. The governance path runs through the Veda/Paladin Safe, timelock, RolesAuthority, and Teller machinery, which is orderly enough to document and centralized enough to matter.

weusd-picwe.title: PicWe USDC Wrapper
weusd-picwe.text: WEUSD is tracked under PicWe (not WEMIX) as a USDC wrapper minted and redeemed 1:1 against USDC, currently trading off-peg near $0.91 despite the documented backing. WEUSD is tracked under PicWe, not WEMIX, because the current documentation and contracts describe PicWe WEUSD. The reserve model is simple today: USDC backing with on-chain {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} rails, while future {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}}/yield collateral stays outside the current scoring assumptions. The off-peg pricing despite documented backing suggests the cross-chain arbitrage loop is not closing efficiently.

gbpe-monerium.title: GBP E-Money Rail
gbpe-monerium.text: GBPe is Monerium's British-pound e-money token, issued under an Icelandic EMI framework rather than a crypto-native collateral game. The reserve story is deliberately dull: safeguarded GBP client funds and permitted EMI reserve assets, with mint and burn handled through KYC'd bank-transfer rails. Pharos still treats the issuer backend and 3-of-6 token-owner Safe as concentrated administration, because regulated does not mean permissionless. For a non-USD stablecoin, that boring bank-rail dependence is the product and the risk; GBPe is useful precisely because it refuses to pretend otherwise.

qcad-stablecorp.title: Regulated CAD Stablecoin
qcad-stablecorp.text: QCAD is a Canadian-dollar stablecoin with the sort of regulatory scaffolding most small fiat tokens can only gesture at: FINTRAC registration, the QCAD Digital Trust framework, and CAD reserves held 1:1 at regulated Canadian institutions. Stablecorp's live balances API gives Pharos real-time supply and reserve totals, which is better than the monthly PDF treasure hunt some issuers still call transparency. The tradeoff is scale and centralization: minting and redemption run through Stablecorp or authorized partners, with Safe-controlled token ownership and upgrade paths rather than permissionless plumbing. For a non-USD stablecoin, QCAD is useful because it is boring in the right places and still small enough that liquidity remains the unglamorous part of the story.

usdxl-last.title: Position-backed synthetic dollar on Hyperliquid
usdxl-last.text: Last USD (USDXL) is a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}}-style synthetic dollar minted on HypurrFi (Aave V3 fork on HyperEVM), drawn against HYPE, HYPE LSTs, UBTC, and ETH collateral with {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} as the only peg defense. Last USD (USDXL) is a crypto-collateralized synthetic dollar minted on HypurrFi, an Aave V3 fork on HyperEVM operated by Last. Users open {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralization{{/term}} borrowing positions against HYPE, HYPE LSTs, bridged BTC (UBTC), and ETH, then draw USDXL against that collateral. It is closer to a {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} than to a 1:1 reserve-backed dollar. Repaying the loan burns the synthetic, and undercollateralized positions are hit with {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}} to defend the peg. Circulating supply sits in the low single-digit millions, with the asset {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}}d between Hyperliquid's HyperEVM (18 decimals) and Hyperliquid L1 spot (8 decimals).

bnusd-balanced.title: The Dollar Left Behind
bnusd-balanced.text: bnUSD is Balanced's cross-chain decentralized dollar, borrowed against {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} positions with a Stability Fund swapping USDC and USDT 1:1 to support the peg. It began life in 2021 as ICON's flagship CDP stablecoin, and that era formally ended on April 7, 2026, when Balanced v2 launched as a cross-chain money market powered by SODAX: the v1 app now exists only for withdrawals, and current issuance runs against a SODAX-wrapped collateral basket spanning Treasury-bill vaults, stablecoins, and a long tail of bridged crypto. Pharos still tracks the legacy ICON-hub deployments, and the report card reads accordingly: backing and economic control hold up in the B range while the exit pillar sits at a flat zero; secondary liquidity has followed the protocol to its new home, leaving the tracked supply technically solvent and practically stranded. The peg itself has never recorded a depeg event, which is the quiet irony: a stablecoin can hold a dollar perfectly while the market that would let you realize that dollar packs up and leaves.

dusd-fluid.title: The Oracle Went Quiet
dusd-fluid.text: Fluid Finance's DUSD was designed as an Arbitrum stablecoin backed by safeguarded bank cash, with an issuer oracle capping minting at the reported off-chain balance. That was a neat bridge between bank reconciliation and smart-contract supply control; it is not the same thing as current proof that the bank accounts, oracle, or redemption rail still operate. Pharos could not verify a recent reserve report, active banking counterparties, live balance publication, or a working {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} route, so the old 'verifiable 24/7' pitch now reads more like historical architecture than present-tense assurance. Single-chain simplicity removes bridge risk but offers little comfort when the evidence path itself has gone quiet. DUSD is a useful reminder that an oracle-enforced ceiling is only as current as the entity still publishing the number.

iusd-initia.title: Initia's AUSD-wrapped ecosystem dollar
iusd-initia.text: Single-chain Initia wrapper of bridged Agora AUSD; reserve yield diverted to ecosystem incentives, redemption routes back through AUSD. iUSD is the native dollar on Initia, the young Move-based Cosmos L1. Each iUSD is backed 1:1 by Agora's AUSD bridged in via LayerZero, so the ultimate reserve trace is Agora's short-dated U.S. Treasuries, repos, and cash custodied at State Street under VanEck management. Unlike standard fiat-backed stables, the reserve yield is redirected by Initia into ecosystem incentives that fund Echelon lending, liquidity programs, and Cabal vaults rather than paid to holders. Supply remains tiny and Initia publishes no attestation for the wrapper itself, so the backing pillar leans on Agora's AUSD transparency and holds up reasonably. The exit pillar fails outright because getting out means a LayerZero bridge hop before Agora's USD redemption window even applies, and that trapped exit is what pins the overall grade at C- despite a spotless peg. Reserve trace runs into AUSD's {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}} and cash at State Street with VanEck-managed {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, with the {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}} layer and Agora's {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} window owning the exit path.

usdcx-movement.title: Movement's native USDC-backed dollar
usdcx-movement.text: USDCx is Movement's native dollar, issued through Circle's xReserve contract: deposit USDC, mint USDCx one-for-one, and move it back out across dozens of chains via CCTP and Gateway without a third-party {{term:bridge}}bridge{{/term}}. The issuer is the key distinction. Move Industries, the team behind Movement, not Circle, issues USDCx, so this is partner-issued plumbing whose solvency is borrowed from Circle's reserves and Circle's {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} rather than owed by Circle to the holder. That borrowing is the entire design and it scores accordingly: the reserve is a single claim on somebody else's stablecoin, and both backing and exit land mid-scale because the wrapper adds smart-contract and venue risk without adding any independent collateral. This release trimmed the grade again by declining to credit an unevidenced supervision claim over the mint; reconciliation against the reserve contract is continuous and observable on-chain, but no independent party is documented as checking it, and Pharos now scores that difference rather than assuming it away. Circulation stays modest, which is the honest read on a token whose job is ecosystem rails for Movement-native DeFi and Global South payment corridors, not a float competing for anyone's treasury.

usdh-hubble.title: Solana's original crypto-backed CDP stablecoin, now dormant
usdh-hubble.text: Hubble's USDH was Solana's first MakerDAO-style {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} stablecoin at 150% min collateral; today it circulates at ~$1.2-1.5M and is structurally dormant. Hubble Protocol's USDH was the first MakerDAO-style {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} stablecoin on Solana, minted against a basket of SOL, mSOL, BTC, and ETH at a minimum 150% collateralization ratio with Stability Pool {{term:liquidation}}liquidations{{/term}}. The protocol launched in 2022, raised $5M from Three Arrows, Crypto.com and others, and originally aspired to challenge centralized stablecoin dominance on Solana. Today USDH circulates at roughly $1.2-1.5M with negligible secondary volume, and the team has pivoted its development energy to sister protocol Kamino Finance. No formal sunset has been announced and the borrow app remains live, but USDH is structurally dormant rather than growing. The 'USDH' symbol is shared with Native Markets and Hermetica. They are three distinct issuers with three distinct collateral models.

zkusd-goal3.title: ZKsync-native sportsbook stablecoin with limited reserve disclosure
zkusd-goal3.text:
A Goal3 sportsbook stable on ZKsync Era, claimed to be overcollateralized but with no itemized backing. Treat it as venue-restricted credit redeemable through one portal.

zkUSD Dollar is the in-house stable issued by Goal3, a sportsbook on ZKsync Era, with circulating supply just over $1M. Goal3 documents the asset as {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} by assets held in the sportsbook, redeemable 1:1 for USDC through the official portal, but the specific accepted collateral, ratios, and on-chain backing addresses are not publicly itemized. Pharos tracks zkUSD primarily for ZKsync ecosystem coverage rather than scale; zkUSD is venue-restricted credit on a single-chain operator, and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} access runs through the Goal3 Portal as the only modeled exit. Secondary liquidity exists on SyncSwap and a small MEXC listing.

ist-agoric.title: Sunset by Governance
ist-agoric.text: IST was Agoric's textbook interchain dollar, built as an {{term:overcollateralization}}overcollateralized{{/term}} {{term:cdp}}CDP{{/term}} against IBC-bridged ATOM and stATOM with Dutch-auction {{term:liquidation}}liquidation{{/term}}, plus a {{term:psm}}PSM{{/term}} swapping approved stablecoins 1:1. It is now a textbook example of how to shut one down. Agoric governance approved a strategic wind-down in spring 2025, ran a roughly 60-day sunset with liquidation fees zeroed so vault users could repay and reclaim collateral, and completed the shutdown on June 26, 2025; Pharos keeps the entry as a frozen archive because nothing mints anymore. The cause of death was not a depeg but a demand problem: an elegantly engineered mechanism on a chain whose DeFi ecosystem never grew large enough to need it. In a cemetery full of stablecoins that died screaming, IST is the rare one that filed the paperwork, gave holders an orderly exit, and turned off the lights. The shutdown made the constraint clear: IST's mechanism was sound, and the chain's ecosystem never generated enough demand for it.

benji-franklin-templeton.title: The Onchain '40 Act Fund
benji-franklin-templeton.text: BENJI is the on-chain share token for Franklin Templeton's FOBXX, an SEC-registered U.S. government {{term:money-market-fund}}money market fund{{/term}} with a stable $1.00 NAV, custodied at JPMorgan Chase with Franklin Templeton as transfer agent and the token as the share record. Yield is distributed by rebasing the holder's share count on-chain rather than letting the price drift, which makes BENJI behave like a par-redeemable dollar even though it is legally a fund share. Business is booming: assets more than quadrupled in the first half of 2026, passing $2.5 billion by July, keeping it the largest tokenised '40 Act {{term:money-market-fund}}MMF{{/term}} in market, with Pharos tracking deployments from Stellar and Ethereum to Solana and Aptos while the BNB Chain and Canton issuances remain unintegrated. The catch is telemetry: reserves run on a curated weekly snapshot of the official factsheet, and since mid-July 2026 Pharos has quarantined the listing and withheld circulating supply and market cap because no permitted runtime source reports a positive figure. A $2.5 billion fund the dashboard cannot cleanly count is the tokenisation story in miniature: the assets are real, the rails are registered, and the data still arrives by factsheet.

sources.label: Crypto Briefing: Franklin Templeton tokenized Treasury fund passes $2.5B (July 2026)

wtgxx-wisdomtree.title: WisdomTree's 24/7 Dealer-Traded Treasury Fund
wtgxx-wisdomtree.text:
A SEC-approved tokenized Treasury MMF trading at a fixed $1 NAV 24/7 through WisdomTree Connect dealers. It is currently quarantined on Pharos because no permitted source reports its on-chain supply.

WTGXX is the digital share class of WisdomTree's Treasury Money Market Digital Fund, renamed from 'Government' in late 2025, a Rule 2a-7 '40 Act-registered {{term:money-market-fund}}money market fund{{/term}} that received SEC approval in early 2026 to support 24/7 dealer trading at a fixed $1.00 NAV, making it one of the most stablecoin-like tokenized MMFs in market. Subscriptions and {{term:redemption}}redemptions{{/term}} are gated to WisdomTree Connect users with USDC dealer settlement and USD-wire alternatives; holdings are short-duration U.S. government obligations: {{term:treasury}}Treasury bills{{/term}}, floating-rate notes, and repos, which are the {{term:rwa}}real-world asset{{/term}} backing. The trouble is visibility, not credit: since mid-July 2026 Pharos has held WTGXX in quarantine because none of its permitted runtime sources report a positive circulating supply or market cap, so the token sits ungraded while the fund side keeps publishing its daily NAV. The share token spans seven networks from Ethereum to Stellar, and Chainlink's NAV feed still prices the reserves. Everything about this fund is measurable except how much of it actually lives on-chain. The '40 Act wrapper solved the trust problem; the telemetry problem turned out to be harder.

sources.label: WisdomTree Treasury Money Market Digital Fund (WTGXX), WisdomTree Connect fund page

vbill-vaneck.title: VanEck's Securitize-Administered Treasury Share
vbill-vaneck.text: VBILL is the on-chain share token for VanEck's Treasury Fund, with Van Eck advising the BVI Professional Fund and Securitize handling administration, tokenization, transfer agency, and KYC. The reserve stack is pleasantly dull: mostly short-duration U.S. T-bills with a cash and repo sleeve, while the token itself accrues NAV rather than rebasing balances. Primary mint and redemption run through Securitize Markets against USDC, AUSD, or wire rails, and the multi-chain footprint is bridged rather than a free-for-all native issuance set. Pharos tracks the live NAV path through the Chainlink NAVLink feed and keeps the product framed as an institutional Treasury share, not a par retail stablecoin. VBILL is the kind of tokenized fund where the boring assets are the feature and the wrapper paperwork is the hobby.

acred-apollo-securitize.title: Private Credit, Not Treasuries
acred-apollo-securitize.text: ACRED is a tokenized, NAV-accreting feeder share into Apollo's diversified private credit fund; backing is illiquid private credit, not T-bills, so the risk profile is medium-to-high rather than cash-like. ACRED is the on-chain feeder share into Apollo Diversified Credit Fund, a multi-strategy private credit portfolio combining direct lending, structured credit, performing credit, and dislocated credit. Unlike BUIDL or BENJI, the collateral is illiquid private credit rather than {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}, so its risk profile is medium-to-high and closer to syrupUSDC than to a stable-NAV vehicle. ACRED is NAV-accreting; primary {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} is monthly at fund NAV through Securitize Markets, supplemented by an on-demand liquidity pool sized to roughly 5% of NAV, and RedStone publishes a NAV oracle used by integrations. Pharos tracks the Ethereum supply contract and flags this asset as a private-credit NAV token rather than a par stablecoin.

eutbl-spiko.title: Europe's First Tokenised T-Bill MMF
eutbl-spiko.text: EUTBL is Spiko's AMF-regulated UCITS short-term {{term:money-market-fund}}MMF{{/term}} backed by Eurozone {{term:treasury}}T-bills{{/term}}: Europe's first tokenized {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} sovereign fund. EUTBL is Spiko's EUR-denominated short-term money market fund: the first AMF-regulated UCITS MMF tokenised on Ethereum. The fund holds short-dated Eurozone sovereign T-bills with weighted average maturity under two months, and EUTBL behaves as a VNAV (variable-NAV) share that accretes value as T-bill yield compounds. Primary subscriptions and redemptions settle same-day at fund NAV with a €1k minimum; Chainlink CCIP bridges issuance to Arbitrum and Polygon. EUTBL is one of Pharos's few EUR-pegged RWA assets and one of the cleanest fits for European institutional users seeking regulatory-grade tokenised cash: a fit that got materially easier to access in June, when Coinbase opened stablecoin-funded subscriptions and redemptions for Spiko's UCITS funds settling on Base.

ustbl-spiko.title: Spiko's USD T-Bill MMF Cousin
ustbl-spiko.text: USTBL is Spiko's USD-denominated AMF-regulated UCITS {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}} holding short-dated U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} bills, deployed across Ethereum, Arbitrum, and Polygon via Chainlink CCIP. USTBL is the USD-denominated sister fund to Spiko's EUTBL. It has the same AMF-regulated UCITS {{term:money-market-fund}}money-market fund{{/term}} architecture, the same ERC-1967 upgradeable proxy, and the same Chainlink CCIP multi-chain rollout (Ethereum, Arbitrum, Polygon), but it holds short-dated U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} bills instead of Eurozone sovereigns. The VNAV share accretes value as T-bill yield compounds, with $1k minimums and same-day NAV settlement. Backed by {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} collateral with institutional {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and AMF {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, USTBL behaves as a {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-bearing{{/term}} share rather than a par stablecoin. The combined Spiko AUM passed $1 billion in late 2025, making the pair one of the larger EU-regulated tokenised treasury franchises in market. Distribution took its biggest step yet in June, when Coinbase opened USDC and EURC subscriptions and redemptions for Spiko's UCITS funds settling on Base. These EU-regulated money-market shares are one tap from an exchange balance.

jtrsy-anemoy.title: S&P's Highest-Rated Tokenised Fund
jtrsy-anemoy.text: BVI Professional Fund holding short-duration U.S. T-bills via Centrifuge ERC-7540; AA+f / S1+ S&P rating, NAV settlement for whitelisted professionals. JTRSY is the Janus Henderson Anemoy Treasury Fund, a BVI Professional Fund where Janus Henderson acts as sub-advisor and Centrifuge handles the on-chain ERC-7540 vault. The fund is rated AA+f / S1+ by S&P, currently the highest credit rating assigned to any tokenised fund. Holdings are short-duration U.S. T-bills; primary subscriptions and redemptions settle same-day at fund NAV for whitelisted non-U.S. Professional Investors via Centrifuge's issuer rail. Distribution extends across Centrifuge V3 to additional chains; Pharos tracks the Ethereum supply contract first, with reserve data curated until Centrifuge's on-chain NAV publishing path is available for automated reserve verification. Holdings are pure short-duration {{term:treasury}}U.S. T-bills{{/term}} held as a tokenized {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} fund share with permissioned Centrifuge {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} and same-day NAV {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}.

bib01-backed.title: Backed's Flagship Treasury Tracker
bib01-backed.text: bIB01 is Backed's NAV-accreting tracker token for the BlackRock iShares 0-1 year U.S. {{term:treasury}}Treasury Bond{{/term}} UCITS ETF, KYC-gated under Swiss DLT Act framework: not pegged to $1. bIB01 is Backed Finance's most-traded tokenised {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} ETF: a Swiss DLT Act-registered tracker certificate that fully backs each token with the BlackRock iShares $ Treasury Bond 0-1yr UCITS ETF (IB01). The token is NAV-accreting and not pegged to $1; price drifts upward continuously as the underlying T-bill ETF accrues yield. Primary mint and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} are KYC-gated through Backed; secondary liquidity is on Uniswap and CoW Protocol. bIB01 deploys on Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain, Polygon, Arbitrum, Gnosis, and Avalanche using the same contract address pattern that Backed uses across its product line.

bc3m-backed.title: Backed's EUR Govt Bond Tracker
bc3m-backed.text: bC3M is Backed's NAV-accreting tracker token for Amundi's short-dated Eurozone government bond UCITS ETF, KYC-gated and registered under Swiss DLT Act, one of the few EUR-pegged {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} tokens. bC3M is Backed Finance's EUR-denominated tokenised tracker certificate fully backed by the AMUNDI GOVIES 0-6 Months Euro Investment Grade UCITS ETF. The token is NAV-accreting in euros, giving Pharos one of the few EUR-pegged RWA assets backed by short-duration Eurozone government bonds, economically the EUR analogue of a {{term:treasury}}Treasury-bond{{/term}} tracker. Same Swiss DLT Act framework as bIB01, same KYC-gated primary issuance through Backed and KYC-gated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}}, same Uniswap / CoW secondary liquidity surfaces. Pharos tracks the Ethereum supply contract first; Backed also publishes the asset on Base, BNB Chain, Polygon, and Gnosis using its multi-chain deployment pattern.

ntbill-nest.title: Nest's On-Plume Treasury Vault
ntbill-nest.text: Nest Credit Treasury vault share on Plume routing into Superstate USTB/USCC and Janus Henderson JTRSY; NAV-accreting fund-of-funds-style token, not a par-redeemable dollar. nTBILL is Nest Credit's {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} vault on Plume: a vault share whose value tracks a curated book of Superstate USTB / USCC and Janus Henderson JTRSY positions, plus a small stablecoin liquidity buffer. The token is NAV-accreting and primary mint/{{term:redemption}}redeem{{/term}} runs through Nest at vault NAV. Reserves are sourced live from the Nest Credit positions API, the same positions source that supports inALPHA. Pharos tracks nTBILL because it references a dollar base, but the token behaves like a tokenised {{term:money-market-fund}}fund-of-funds{{/term}} share rather than a par-redeemable stablecoin.

nbasis-nest.title: Nest's Basis-Trade Vault
nbasis-nest.text: Nest Credit basis-trade vault token combining tokenized T-bill collateral with perpetual shorts; NAV-accreting rather than $1-pegged, value drifts with funding-rate performance. nBASIS is Nest Credit's {{term:basis-trade}}basis-trade{{/term}} strategy vault: tokenised {{term:treasury}}T-bill{{/term}} collateral combined with {{term:perpetual}}perpetual{{/term}} short positions, rebalanced by Nest. Closer in profile to Ethena USDe or Midas mRe7YIELD than to a par stablecoin. The token's value drifts with {{term:funding-rate}}funding-rate{{/term}} performance rather than holding $1. Pharos lists it because the strategy references the dollar as its base and the Nest Credit positions API publishes live NAV, but the methodology treats nBASIS as a strategy vault with high collateral-quality risk and a NAV-token notice.

nopal-nest.title: Nest's BlackOpal Credit Vault
nopal-nest.text: Nest Credit vault token wrapping BlackOpal LiquidStone II tokenized private-credit positions plus a small liquidity buffer; NAV-accreting vault share, not a par-redeemable stablecoin. nOPAL is Nest Credit's BlackOpal LiquidStone II vault: tokenised private-credit positions plus a small {{term:treasury}}Treasury{{/term}} and stablecoin liquidity buffer. Like other Nest vaults, the token is NAV-accreting and primary access runs through Nest at vault NAV. Pharos flags nOPAL as a private-credit vault share rather than a par stablecoin; the high-risk reserve slice reflects the underlying LiquidStone II credit positions classified as {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}}-adjacent exposure.

nwisdom-nest.title: Nest's WisdomTree-Backed Vault
nwisdom-nest.text: Nest Credit vault share built around WisdomTree Connect tokenized fund exposure (xCRDYX) plus an nTBILL liquidity buffer; NAV-accreting tokenized fund share, not a par stablecoin. nWISDOM is Nest Credit's vault built around WisdomTree's tokenised fund shares (xCRDYX and related WisdomTree Connect products) with a small nTBILL and stablecoin liquidity buffer, classified as {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}}-adjacent vault exposure. Yield accretes through the underlying WisdomTree fund NAV; primary mint/{{term:redemption}}redeem{{/term}} runs through Nest at vault NAV. Pharos tracks it on the same live reserves pattern as inALPHA, with the understanding that the token is a vault share rather than a par stablecoin.

susdc-spark.title: Spark's USDC share class on the Sky savings rate
susdc-spark.text: Spark Savings USDC lets USDC holders take the Sky savings rate without first converting into USDS, with idle deposits pulled out and deployed by the Spark Liquidity Layer. Unlike the immutable Morpho vaults it competes with, spUSDC is a UUPS proxy whose mint-critical logic can be replaced through Sky's forty-eight-hour governance pause. It is visible, delayed, and still a live upgrade path. That is why the card was already held below its peers by a cap covering an upgrade-control address it shares with another tracked asset; this release simply replaced that constraint with a lower one, dropping economic control to the mint floor once the supervision claim over that mint failed to produce evidence. Backing did not move at all, because Pharos never credited spUSDC with Circle's reserve in the first place: the slice is scored as an aggregate Spark protocol position, not as USDC sitting still. So the D is a single-pillar verdict, and the pillar is the one about who can change the rules. For a savings passthrough, that was the only question that mattered. It remains convenient, and it remains not independent.

susdt-spark.title: USDT-denominated Spark Savings vault on the Sky rate
susdt-spark.text: Spark Savings USDT is the Tether-denominated version of Spark's savings passthrough into the Sky Savings Rate. The wrapper gives USDT holders a rising share price, but the risk stack includes Spark and inherits Tether issuer exposure, Spark vault mechanics, Sky governance rate decisions, and whatever liquidity the vault and PSM can actually supply on withdrawal. That is a lot of institutional and protocol trust to package as one tidy ERC-4626 receipt. Pharos treats spUSDT separately from spUSDC because changing the underlying issuer changes the dependency surface, even if the vault interface looks nearly identical. Same savings plumbing, different centralized dollar underneath.

sgho-aave.title: Aave's non-slashable GHO savings module
sgho-aave.text:
Aave Savings GHO (sGHO) is an ERC-4626 savings vault on Ethereum whose shares increase in GHO value as yield accrues. Deposits mint shares at the prevailing exchange rate, so one sGHO does not represent a fixed one GHO. The governance-set savings rate accrues on-chain, replacing the legacy sGHO product's separately claimed Merit rewards. Deposited GHO stays in the vault, while the DAO funds yield separately.

The savings vault is non-slashable and distinct from Umbrella stkGHO, whose stakers absorb GHO-market deficits. Shares can be redeemed for GHO without a cooldown, subject to the vault's pause controls. Pharos records GHO as the wrapper's single backing asset, so the savings layer adds no collateral diversification. Holders remain exposed to GHO's underlying collateral and peg risk, alongside the vault's smart-contract controls and governance decisions over the savings rate.

gtusdcp-gauntlet.title: Gauntlet's curated USDC MetaMorpho V2 vault
gtusdcp-gauntlet.text: Gauntlet USDC Prime is the V2 line: three immutable MetaMorpho deployments across Ethereum, Base, and Arbitrum, turning USDC into curated exposure over permissioned Morpho Blue markets backed by blue-chip crypto, RWA, and yield-bearing collateral. Immutability is the strongest thing on the card: the parameter Safes steer allocations and nothing else, though Arbitrum's runs at a three-of-seven threshold where the other two require four, an asymmetry that says more about deployment convenience than intent. The drop to D is procedural rather than portfolio-driven: the mint supervision claim produced no evidence and no longer earns credit, so economic control sits at the floor for minting nobody independently reconciles, while backing and exit finished the release untouched. Share price still appreciates on borrower interest, and withdrawals still depend on Morpho liquidity and on the curator not having optimized the book into a queue at the wrong moment; none of that changed either. What changed is that the vault is now scored on its paperwork rather than on its reputation, and the paperwork was thinner than the reputation.

gtusdc-gauntlet.title: Gauntlet's conservative USDC MetaMorpho vault
gtusdc-gauntlet.text: gtUSDC is the Ethereum-only V1 Morpho Prime vault curated by Gauntlet, an ERC-4626 wrapper compounding {{term:yield-bearing}}lending yield{{/term}} across vetted USDC markets on Morpho Blue. It is deliberately the conservative end of what a curated lending book can look like. Pharos tracks it apart from the V2 vault at a different address for the same reason it separates Steakhouse's USDC and USDT books, and this release rather undercut the point by moving both in lockstep anyway. The fall to D does not reflect Gauntlet's allocations or the collateral. Backing scores exactly where it did before, and the dollar underneath never moved. The grade reflects evidence: supervision of the vault's mint was asserted rather than demonstrated, unevidenced supervision now scores as none, and economic control lands on the floor, taking a card that had been resting comfortably against its parent ceiling straight down through it. There is a particular irony in a risk-modelling firm's flagship vault being marked down for undocumented controls rather than bad markets, and that is the kind of gap that is cheap to close and expensive to leave open.

yvusdc-yearn.title: Yearn USDC Vault
yvusdc-yearn.text: yvUSDC-1 is the canonical Yearn v3 USDC vault: an ERC-4626 {{term:yield-bearing}}share token{{/term}} whose price appreciates as Yearn's allocator rotates capital across governance-whitelisted strategies. The whitelist is broader than the book. Funded allocation has narrowed onto the Sky ecosystem with the Morpho leg revoked, so diversification here is a governance option rather than a present fact. Nothing moved this release: minting is deposit-only, the mint review closed out cleanly, and exits still queue against aggregate strategy liquidity, which matters in a drawdown. The interesting fact is the one that never moves: the A- is not Yearn's own arithmetic but a ceiling, the rule that a child cannot rate above the parent it requires. Every pillar on this card scores well above the grade the card is permitted to carry, which is the dependency graph doing exactly what it exists to do: hold a wrapper and you hold the wrapped thing's rating, on someone else's schedule.

aa-falconx-mev-capital.title: FalconX Credit Vault
aa-falconx-mev-capital.text: AA_FalconXUSDC is a Pareto credit-vault tranche: not a Falcon Finance stablecoin and not a MEV Capital strategy token, despite the naming fog. The underlying exposure is USDC lent into FalconX institutional credit lines through a bankruptcy-remote SPV curated by M11 Credit, so the real risk is private-credit performance and monthly exit timing rather than peg arbitrage. This release ran its evidence through the mint-authority gate and it held: the tranche cannot mint itself outside the IdleCDO deposit path, and its supervision and reconciliation claims were bound to structural chain proofs rather than downgraded, which is more than most wrappers managed this cycle. The card finished where it started, and the C is earned honestly: an exit pillar with no comparable same-notional route out, and a backing pillar flagged because the reserve review covers only part of the envelope, since no source publishes obligor or instrument weights for the underlying book. This is a lender's balance sheet tokenized, and the word USDC in the symbol should not lull anyone into reading it as cash.

vndc-jade-labs.title: VNDC Quarantined VND Token
vndc-jade-labs.text: VNDC spent years as the only VND stablecoin with material market presence, which makes its 2026 collapse into quarantine the more instructive. Vietnamese authorities arrested ONUS/VNDC-linked executives in March 2026 in a fraud and money-laundering investigation, with local reporting describing platform withdrawal disruptions, so {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} and reserve claims moved from weakly attested to actively suspect. The disclosures had already shifted under holders' feet: VNDC 2.0 describes USDT/USDC smart-contract collateral pools rather than the VND bank {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} of the original pitch, self-reported by an issuer whose own website has been unreachable on repeated checks. Pharos quarantined the listing on 2026-07-15 because no permitted runtime source still reports a positive circulating supply or market cap. The aggregator figures that once diverged from on-chain supply now simply are not there. A dong rail that cannot prove its own existence is only a claim, and the people behind it are answering to prosecutors.

hkdr-rd-technologies.title: Missed the First Wave, Still in the Race
hkdr-rd-technologies.text: Pre-launch HKD stablecoin from RD Technologies; in HKMA sandbox but missed the April 2026 first licence cohort. HKDR is the HKD stablecoin from RD Technologies, a Hong Kong fintech founded by former HKMA chief executive Norman Chan. Its subsidiary RD InnoTech was in the first July 2024 cohort admitted to the HKMA stablecoin issuer sandbox, where it tested digital-asset trading rails and cross-border trade payments; the firm has been positioning for licensing under the Stablecoins Ordinance that took effect August 1 2025. On 2026-04-10 the HKMA gazetted the first stablecoin issuer licences (FRS01 and FRS02) to Anchorpoint and HSBC, with RD InnoTech absent from that cohort. RD remains a credible later-license contender. A recent Series A2 round and a memorandum of understanding with ZA Bank both point to a serious operational build-out, but the regulatory window has shifted to a slower queue. The entry remains pre-launch until licence issuance is confirmed. The eventual product still routes through HKMA-mandated {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}}, segregated {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, and a regulated {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} window.

brd-volpon.title: Selic-Linked Yield, In a Token
brd-volpon.text: BRD is a pre-launch Brazilian real stablecoin from CF Inovacao, backed by Brazilian {{term:treasury}}Treasury bonds{{/term}} and structured to pass Selic-rate yield back to holders. BRD is a BRL stablecoin announced January 6 2026 by Tony Volpon, a former deputy governor of the Central Bank of Brazil, through his company CF Inovacao. The distinctive structural choice: BRD is backed by Brazilian National Treasury bonds and explicitly designed to pass the Selic-linked yield (currently around 15%) back to holders, rather than retaining it as issuer revenue. That is the same model Crown's BRLV already operates in institutional channels; Crown raised $13.5M from Paradigm in December 2025, but BRD is positioning as the first to make {{term:yield-bearing}}yield-sharing{{/term}} the primary product framing rather than a niche feature. The competitive set in Brazilian BRL stablecoins is small but real: Transfero BRZ ($185M), BBRL ($51M), BRL1, plus cREAL on Celo. The harder gate is Brazilian regulation: BCB's FX-classification regime took effect February 2 2026 and final Consulta Publica 111 output is still pending, which is why Volpon has not published a launch date alongside the announcement.

krw1-bdacs.title: Korea's First Bank-Backed Won Stablecoin, Stuck in PoC
krw1-bdacs.text: BDACS/Woori KRW PoC on Avalanche with real-time banking-API reserve attestation; commercial gating awaits Korea's Digital Asset Basic Act. KRW1 is BDACS's KRW-backed stablecoin, developed with Woori Bank as the reserve custodian and launched on Avalanche in September 2025, but in a proof-of-concept phase, not in public circulation. The structural advantages are real: real-time banking-API reserve attestation through Woori, KISA's endorsement of Avalanche for public-sector reliability, and a February 2026 Plume partnership that positions KRW1 as the Korean institutional settlement rail for tokenized RWAs (Plume hosts roughly $645M in tokenized assets). The commercial gating is Korea's still-pending Digital Asset Basic Act framework, where BDACS is explicitly trying to make KRW1 the technical standard. The strategic weakness is distribution. BDACS is a B2B custodian without a consumer app or retail footprint, which makes KRW1 likely to win on the institutional side and lose to bank-led or super-app issuers if Korea's eventual framework favours retail surfaces. Real-time banking-API {{term:attestation}}attestation{{/term}} runs through Woori Bank {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}}, with KRW1 positioning itself as the settlement rail for Korean institutional {{term:rwa}}RWA{{/term}} flows and {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} routed through regulated banking channels.

rusd-revolut.title: Revolut Dollar Precedent From EURR
rusd-revolut.text: Revolut's USD stablecoin is still unannounced, and the August 2026 launch of its euro sibling made the shape of any dollar token considerably clearer, mostly by invalidating the assumption everyone was working from. The legal substrate looked settled: a MiCA CASP licence from CySEC in October 2025, plus Revolut's Bank-of-Lithuania EMI supplying the e-money-token issuer foundation MiCA Title IV requires. Then Revolut shipped EURR on August 26 and the issuer of record turned out to be Bridge Building S.A., the Luxembourg entity of Stripe-owned Bridge, under a CSSF licence, with Revolut Digital Assets Europe merely distributing. Europe's largest neobank, holding every licence it needed to issue in-house, chose to rent the issuance instead. That reframes RUSD: the nearest live precedent for a Revolut dollar is a third-party regulated-issuer relationship, which trades balance-sheet control and reserve-disclosure ownership for speed to market. It also means the interesting counterparty question for RUSD is no longer whether Vilnius signs off, but whether Revolut is content to have Stripe's infrastructure sitting between its 65 million users and their {{term:redemption}}redemption{{/term}} rights. Revolut's US path runs separately through an OCC charter application targeting a 2027 launch with stablecoin services from day one: third-party tokens, not confirmed own issuance. Ticker, chain, issuer entity, and reserve and {{term:custody}}custody{{/term}} disclosure model for a USD token all remain unannounced, and the euro launch suggests that reserve disclosure and custody will be the key uncertainties.

sources.label: FinTech Futures: Revolut launches euro-backed stablecoin EURR
Blockhead: Revolut launches EURR as it cuts off Tether across Europe

brl-itau.title: Brazil's Biggest Bank Waits for the Rulebook
brl-itau.text: BRL-ITAU is a pre-launch stablecoin under evaluation by Brazil's largest private bank Itau Unibanco, with peg currency and design pending BCB regulation.
